records.text: Introduction
records.all_revision_text: Introduction

records.text: The high-voltage substations and transmission lines in Southern California face serious seismic threats. When earthquakes damage the electric system, neighborhoods in the region would experience a varying range of levels and durations of impacts, as the local access to electricity depends on which substations remain functional and how quickly they can be repaired.
records.all_revision_text: The high-voltage substations and transmission lines in Southern California face serious seismic threats. When earthquakes damage the electric system, neighborhoods in the region would experience a varying range of levels and durations of impacts, as the local access to electricity depends on which substations remain functional and how quickly they can be repaired.

records.text: Evaluating post-earthquake power restoration is important because electricity is essential for economic and social activities, especially in densely populated urban areas. Since the impacts of earthquakes are not spatially uniform, an evaluation framework should quantify the impacts through population-weighted recovery indicators, tract-level restoration dispersion, time to restore hospital service, equity in restoration waiting times, network criticality of affected assets, and estimates of the loss in power supply at the network and substation levels.

records.text: This project identifies and analyzes such unequal levels of exposure and recovery across the census tracts in the City of Los Angeles by modeling the power grid as a network of supply and demand: substations on the supply side, census tracts on the demand side, connected by tract-specific “supply weights.” This project questions which substations are structurally critical for tract-level power service, how selected damage scenarios propagate through that network, and how different repair priorities influence the size of the population served by restoration.

records.text: Literature Review
records.all_revision_text: Literature Review

records.text: Among the literature on modeling earthquake risks, the recent studies by Soleimani et al. (2021) and Cheng et al. (2024) introduce novel approaches to simulate scenarios realistically. Soleimani et al. develop a multihazard method to measure earthquake risk to avoid any hazard type overrepresenting the model and results. They first map each earthquake’s ground shaking, liquefaction, and surface fault rupture to create consistent hazard maps. From a large set of possible ruptures, they screen events based on their contribution to overall risk. They then use a mixed-integer linear program to select a smaller set of representative ruptures with probabilities that reproduce the full hazard distribution. This smaller set is resampled to generate the final collection of scenarios. In a case study on the City of Los Angeles, the 351 selected scenarios produce results matching the simulations based on the full rupture set, which reduces computation time while maintaining accuracy (Soleimani et al., 2021).

records.text: Moving forward, Cheng et al. (2024) simulate 351 earthquake scenarios generated by Soleimani et al. (2021), each with 12 possible damage outcomes, to model the seismic risk in the City of Los Angeles at the census tract level. They employ the HAZUS risk modeling tool developed by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) with a Direct Current (DC) load flow model to track delivered power and load shedding (the intentional limiting or closing of power supply to prevent system overloading) over a nine-period restoration timeline. Cheng et al. find that substation damage causes most of the outages, generator damage causes secondary effects, and transmission line damage makes minimal impacts. The pattern concentrates the risks of load shedding in northern and central Los Angeles tracts. In addition, Cheng et al. map system-level outages to census tracts through distance-weighted allocation. Modeling the solar plus storage adoption levels of  2030, they suggest that solar plus storage reduces early-stage load shedding, but the benefits are uneven and favor higher-income, homeowner-occupied areas (Cheng et al., 2024).

records.text: Literature that models the impacts of earthquakes on the electrical grid include the works by Shinozuka et al. (2007) and Johnson et al. (2020), both applying Monte Carlo simulation (MCS). Shinozuka et al. first calculate the Peak Ground Acceleration (PGA), a measure of earthquake intensity, at 52 receiving stations across 50 scenarios of historic earthquakes in the City of Los Angeles, such as the 1994 Northridge earthquake that made the city black out for the first time in history. Shinozuka et al. then model fragility curves, each representing the probability that a component fails given a certain PGA (Shinozuka et al., 2007). The fragility curves simulate how individual components may be damaged and generate 20 different possible outcomes of network damage for each scenario of earthquakes, reflecting a standard MCS practice of repeated trials (Radu et al., 2018). In turn, they employ power flow analysis to check how earthquakes disrupt power supply, fluctuate voltages, and disconnect transmission lines to quantify the network stability (Shinozuka et al., 2007). Similarly, Johnson et al. use fragility curves to estimate the likelihood that individual grid components fail under specific levels of seismic shaking. Their MCS then randomly samples component failure states based on each selected earthquake scenario’s fragility curve. It allows them to analyze the resulting damaged grid with a power flow solver to calculate Demand Not Served (DNS), or the loss of power supply (Johnson et al.,2020).

records.text: Studies by Çag˘nan et. al (2006) and Xu et al. (2007) cover methodologies to model the post-earthquake restoration of power systems. Çag˘nan et. al (2006) combine a seismic hazard model, a damage model developed using fragility curves and MCS, and a discrete-event restoration simulation that tracks inspections, repairs, crew travel, and resource constraints. Running multiple MCS scenarios, Çag˘nan et. al produce restoration curves that show how quickly power is restored and identify risks of long outages, uneven recovery across zones, and shortages in crews or equipment. Çag˘nan et. al show that increasing repair crews most effectively reduces long-duration outages, and they reflect considerations for equitable restoration across geographies (Çag˘nan et. al, 2006). Similarly, Xu et al. (2007) simulate post-earthquake recovery of the Los Angeles power system by scheduling inspections, damage assessments, and repairs across substations to reduce outages. They use restoration curves to track how power recovers after disruptions. The model by Xu et al. minimizes the average outage, measured by SAIDIEQ (the area above the restoration curve). They use a genetic algorithm to schedule tasks and evaluate the resulting recovery in a simulation, which reduces total outage time compared to standard approaches (Xu et al., 2007).

records.text: Cavdaroglu et al. (2013) introduce a model of restoration task scheduling that supports realistic modeling of repair crews’ travel time and path. Cavdaroglu et al. frame recovery as a co-optimization process of repairs, crew assignment, and scheduling, depending on abstractions of travel time, precedence, and repair uncertainty. Their model prioritizes repairs based on the amount of service restored per unit time and allocates tasks to crews to accelerate overall system restoration (Cavdaroglu et al., 2013).

records.text: Despite the extensive literature, three methodological gaps challenge the application of existing models in real-world disaster response:
records.all_revision_text: Despite the extensive literature, three methodological gaps challenge the application of existing models in real-world disaster response:

records.text: Disconnection Between Physical Damage and Functional Restoration: Existing frameworks often rely on deterministic repair tables (e.g., HAZUS) that conflate physical repair (which takes weeks) with functional restoration (which takes hours/days via grid redundancy). This "physics-only" approach systematically overestimates outage durations compared to historical records (e.g., Northridge 1994).
records.all_revision_text: Disconnection Between Physical Damage and Functional Restoration: Existing frameworks often rely on deterministic repair tables (e.g., HAZUS) that conflate physical repair (which takes weeks) with functional restoration (which takes hours/days via grid redundancy). This "physics-only" approach systematically overestimates outage durations compared to historical records (e.g., Northridge 1994).

records.text: Fragmentation of Fragility and Logistics Models: Current research operates in silos: engineering studies (e.g., Cheng et al., 2024) quantify damage but ignore post-disaster resource bottlenecks, while operations research studies (e.g., Xu et al., 2007) optimize scheduling but lack hazard-consistent damage inputs. There is a lack of integrated frameworks that couple stochastic fragility modeling with resource-constrained queuing simulations.

There is a lack of integrated frameworks that couple stochastic fragility modeling with resource-constrained queuing simulations.

records.text: Absence of Equity-Centric Scheduling Evaluation: Traditional recovery metrics focus on aggregate efficiency (e.g., minimizing total system downtime), masking spatial disparities that affect vulnerable communities. This study quantifies how specific engineering prioritization strategies (e.g., prioritizing hospitals vs. population ce) contribute to inequality at the granular census tract level, as suggested in the study by Cheng et al. (2024).

Crucially, these physical damage states are mapped to functional restoration times rather than generic repair averages.

records.text: Data and Methods
records.all_revision_text: Data and Methods

records.text: This study establishes a multi-layered computational framework to evaluate the seismic resilience of the Los Angeles power grid, integrating critical infrastructure topology, seismological hazard modeling, and socio-demographic vulnerability. The physical network model synthesizes substation geolocation data from OpenStreetMap with high-voltage transmission geometries from the California Energy Commission (CEC) to define a topologically valid graph. To capture spatially distributed hazards, we utilize USGS ShakeMaps to assign scenario-specific Peak Ground Acceleration (PGA) intensities to each network node. We examine three historical earthquake scenarios—the 1933 Long Beach, 1971 San Fernando, and 1994 Northridge events—selected to represent diverse seismotectonic sources and distinct spatial damage footprints ranging from regional disruptions to citywide blackouts.

To capture spatially distributed hazards, we utilize USGS ShakeMaps to assign scenario-specific Peak Ground Acceleration (PGA) intensities to each network node. We examine three historical earthquake scenarios—the 1933 Long Beach, 1971 San Fernando, and 1994 Northridge events—selected to represent diverse seismotectonic sources and distinct spatial damage footprints ranging from regional disruptions to citywide blackouts.

records.text: The societal dimension of these disruptions is assessed by overlaying the physical grid onto U.S. Census Bureau tract boundaries, populated with American Community Survey (ACS) demographic data and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) scores to quantify equity in recovery. Furthermore, human mobility dynamics are incorporated using Origin-Destination (OD) trip data from Replica, enabling the estimation of "flow loss" where travel is impeded by power outages.

Furthermore, human mobility dynamics are incorporated using Origin-Destination (OD) trip data from Replica, enabling the estimation of "flow loss" where travel is impeded by power outages.

records.text: The simulation pipeline progresses through three analytical stages. First, stochastic fragility modeling maps local PGA values to discrete substation damage states via lognormal fragility functions, using Monte Carlo simulation to sample probabilistic failure modes and physical repair times. Second, network criticality analysis evaluates structural robustness using graph metrics (e.g., degree and betweenness) and impact-based measures quantifying the fragmentation of the Largest Connected Component (LCC). Finally, functional restoration is simulated under two regimes: a theoretical unconstrained baseline and a realistic, resource-constrained scheduling model involving 28 repair crews dispatched from 7 bases with explicit travel-time modeling. Within this constrained environment, we evaluate the efficacy of four prioritization strategies—Random, Centrality-first, Impact-first (Population), and Hospital-first—aggregating component-level repairs into system-level recovery curves. The analysis concludes by classifying census tracts into resilience typologies using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and K-Means clustering, thereby identifying distinct vulnerability profiles based on recovery performance and socio-demographic characteristics.

records.text: Data Preparation
records.all_revision_text: Data Preparation

records.text: The foundation of the simulation is the integration of heterogeneous geospatial datasets. The physical power grid is represented by substation point inventories and high-voltage transmission line geometries synthesized from California Energy Commission (CEC) and Homeland Infrastructure Foundation-Level Data (HIFLD) sources. To characterize seismic hazards, we assign scenario-specific Peak Ground Acceleration (PGA) values to each substation by sampling spatially interpolated ShakeMap fields. Census tracts serve as the fundamental unit of analysis, represented by attributes including geometry, population, Social Vulnerability Index (SVI), National Risk Index (NRI) and hospital locations. The study area is set within the City of Los Angeles administrative boundaries.

records.text: Topological Reconstruction of the Transmission Network
records.all_revision_text: Topological Reconstruction of the Transmission Network

records.text: Transforming raw GIS geometries into a mathematically valid network graph G is a critical prerequisite for subsequent analysis. MultiLineString of Transmission lines are first broken into LineString segments, whose endpoints are snapped to the nearest substation coordinates within a spatial tolerance of 300 m using a KD-tree index. Transmission lines passing through substations without explicit vertices are split at intersection points to ensure that all substations function as active nodes within the topology. An undirected weighted MultiGraph is then constructed using the vertices in LineStrings and edges connecting every consecutive vertex. This serves as a model representation of the real transmission graph. Substations are snapped to the nearest graph node. The substation-substation distances are then calculated by Dijkstra shortest path on graph G.

records.text: The topological graph requires straight connection between each pair of directly connected substations, instead of the real geometry. A pair is considered directly adjacent only if the vertices listed in the shortest path are not associated with any other substation. An undirected edge is then constructed between directly adjacent pairs with the weight being the calculated along-grid shortest path.

records.text: Service-weighted criticality: population-based impact
records.all_revision_text: Service-weighted criticality: population-based impact

records.text: Beyond purely structural notions of node importance, a service-weighted impact metric that expresses connectivity degradation in terms of the population potentially affected is considered. This metric leverages the tract–substation coupling table to assign each substation an “attributed population” based on fractional service dependence. Specifically, for each mapping record linking tract t to substation i with weight wt,i and tract population popt, we define the population assignment to substation i as popt wt,i. Summing over all mapped tracts yields the total population attributed to each substation, and the system total is total_pop=tpopt.

records.text: E. Resource-Constrained Recovery and System Synthesis

records.text: Resource-Constrained Dispatch Model
records.all_revision_text: Resource-Constrained Dispatch Model

records.text: We model post-earthquake restoration as a resource-constrained Multi-Depot Vehicle Routing and Scheduling Problem (MDVRSP). Let S be the set of all substations, and let J⊆S denote the subset classified as damaged in a given Monte Carlo realization. A finite workforce of K=28 repair crews is distributed across D=7maintenance depots. Each crew k∈{1,…,K} is anchored to a home depot d(k)∈D at initialization and executes a time-ordered sequence of repair tasks.
records.all_revision_text: We model post-earthquake restoration as a resource-constrained Multi-Depot Vehicle Routing and Scheduling Problem (MDVRSP). Let S be the set of all substations, and let J⊆S denote the subset classified as damaged in a given Monte Carlo realization. A finite workforce of K=28 repair crews is distributed across D=7maintenance depots. Each crew k∈{1,…,K} is anchored to a home depot d(k)∈D at initialization and executes a time-ordered sequence of repair tasks.

records.text: State variables. At any decision epoch, each crew is characterized by its current location (either a depot or the most recently completed substation), and its next-available time. The system state is defined by the set of remaining unrepaired damaged substations and the crew states. Each damaged substation j∈J is a single indivisible task that can be served by exactly one crew; parallel work on a single substation is not modeled.
records.all_revision_text: State variables. At any decision epoch, each crew is characterized by its current location (either a depot or the most recently completed substation), and its next-available time. The system state is defined by the set of remaining unrepaired damaged substations and the crew states. Each damaged substation j∈J is a single indivisible task that can be served by exactly one crew; parallel work on a single substation is not modeled.

records.text: Travel-time coupling. Spatial frictions are modeled through a precomputed impedance matrix τ(a,b) (hours) between any two locations a,b∈D∪S. These travel times are computed from shortest paths on a routable OpenStreetMap road graph, ensuring that dispatch decisions reflect the actual topology of the Los Angeles transportation network rather than straight-line distances. The travel-time matrix is treated as fixed for a given analysis run. It does not depend on time of day or post-event road degradation unless explicitly modeled elsewhere.

records.text: Operational constraints. The formulation enforces (i) crew capacity: at most K concurrent repairs, one per crew; (ii) precedence in time: a crew cannot start a task until it has completed its prior task and traveled to the new site; and (iii) geographic feasibility: crews begin at their assigned depots and move along the road network, incurring travel time between consecutive tasks.
records.all_revision_text: Operational constraints. The formulation enforces (i) crew capacity: at most K concurrent repairs, one per crew; (ii) precedence in time: a crew cannot start a task until it has completed its prior task and traveled to the new site; and (iii) geographic feasibility: crews begin at their assigned depots and move along the road network, incurring travel time between consecutive tasks.

records.text: Because the full MDVRSP is NP-hard at realistic network scales, we do not attempt an exact optimization. Instead, we evaluate a family of policy-driven greedy heuristics within a discrete-event simulation, which allows transparent comparisons among prioritization strategies while preserving the key physical constraints.

records.text: Event Logic and Scheduling Timeline
records.all_revision_text: Event Logic and Scheduling Timeline

records.text: Recovery is simulated using a logistics-aware Discrete-Event Simulation (DES) that advances time by operational events rather than fixed time steps. Two event types are sufficient to define the restoration timeline: Crew availability (decision event) occurs when a crew becomes free to accept a new assignment at time t. Repair completion (state-change event) occurs when a substation transitions to the functional state at the instant its repair finishes.

records.text: Figure 7: Correlations of Degree, Betweenness, and Impact Centralities
records.all_revision_text: Figure 7: Correlations of Degree, Betweenness, and Impact Centralities

records.text: Figure 7 reports pairwise correlations among structural centrality measures (degree, closeness, and betweenness) and two consequence-oriented measures (impact centrality and impact population). The structural metrics are moderately to strongly correlated, with degree most closely correlating with closeness (r = 0.71) and more moderate correlations between betweenness and both closeness (r = 0.59) and degree (r = 0.51). In contrast, impact centrality is largely decoupled from simple connectivity and reachability, showing near-zero correlation with degree (r = 0.07) and a weak correlation with closeness (r = 0.17), but a moderate relationship with betweenness (r = 0.59), consistent with bridge-like substations driving disproportionate consequences. Impact population is moderately correlated with impact centrality (r = 0.67) and also relates to betweenness (r = 0.51) more than to degree (r = 0.06), indicating that population exposure is better captured by network position and flow importance than by node degree alone.

records.text: The results indicate that substation importance depends on which centrality is considered. Degree centrality captures local connectivity, but a high degree does not reliably translate into systemwide consequence. Betweenness centrality highlights bridge nodes that concentrate shortest-path routing and therefore represent potential bottlenecks. Impact centrality directly reflects fragmentation risk by measuring how much network connectivity contracts when a node is removed, and its weak correlation with degree and closeness suggests that the most disruptive substations are not always the most connected or the most accessible. Taken together, these centralities imply that restoration priorities should be guided by nodes with high impact centrality and, secondarily, high betweenness centrality, rather than high degree alone.

records.text: When the power grid fragments into disconnected sub-networks, transmission lines would no longer connect the available supply to demand across those sub-networks, so power outage can persist even if some local assets remain functional.

records.text: The percolation curves in Figure 11 track the largest connected component (LCC) fraction as substations are removed. Under random removal, connectivity decreases gradually at first, and then drops more sharply by around 0.4 as the 25th - 30th nodes are removed. Thereafter the LCC fraction stabilizes above 0.1 until more than 40 nodes are randomly removed.

records.text: In contrast, the targeted attack (impact/λ₂-targeted) removes nodes ranked by impact centrality, so each removal is chosen to maximally reduce global connectivity. As a result, the LCC fraction falls much faster: within the first 15 targeted removals, the LCC fraction drops to roughly 0.25, long before the random case reaches comparable degradation. After this early collapse, the remaining nodes are largely in smaller components, so additional removals produce smaller changes until the LCC eventually decays toward 0 after around 35 nodes are removed. The two percolation curves indicate that the network is substantially more vulnerable to failures at a small set of high-impact substations than to the same number of random outages.

records.text: Conclusion
records.all_revision_text: Conclusion

records.text: This project presents a comprehensive pipeline to evaluate earthquake impacts on electric transmission-grid functionality and tract-level outcomes. A topological representation of the transmission network is constructed to support substation centrality and criticality analysis. For three earthquake scenarios, scenario-specific intensity fields are assigned to substations, fragility functions are applied to estimate probabilistic substation damage states, and a tract-substation mapping matrix propagates substation disruption into census-tract outage probabilities, producing spatially explicit impact maps. Recovery across scenarios is then simulated and compared using power-supply restoration and network-robustness metrics under both unconstrained and logistics-aware restoration conditions. The project concludes with principal component analysis (PCA) and k-means clustering to classify census tracts into resilience typologies based on simulated recovery outcomes and socio-economic attributes.

Recovery across scenarios is then simulated and compared using power-supply restoration and network-robustness metrics under both unconstrained and logistics-aware restoration conditions. The project concludes with principal component analysis (PCA) and k-means clustering to classify census tracts into resilience typologies based on simulated recovery outcomes and socio-economic attributes.

records.text: Overall, the City of Los Angeles power grid forms a connected, highly clustered small-world network, so restoring a relatively small set of structurally important substations can rapidly improve systemwide connectivity. However, which substations count as “important” depends on the centrality metric used (e.g., degree vs. betweenness vs. impact), and these network-based priorities do not necessarily coincide with equity-priority considerations. In our simulation of the the 1933 Long Beach, the 1971 San Fernando, and the 1994 Northridge earthquake scenarios, the Northridge creates the most damage and requires the longest time for reparation. Across scenarios, prioritizing the repair of substations with high Degree Centrality or Betweenness Centrality and those serving hospitals are shown to be the most efficient strategies for the system service recovery to 50%.

records.text: Results suggest the following three restoration schemes targeting different objectives. For efficient restoration of the power-grid network, the City should prioritize substations with high degree to reconnect large portions of the network quickly or high betweenness to protect bridge nodes that maintain global connectivity. For efficient restoration of electricity service to the population, the City should prioritize substations that serve tracts containing hospitals, paired with high-degree substations for faster restoration of connectivity, as well as high-betweenness substations to preserve cross-area connectivity and prevent the grid from splitting into isolated components. For equitable restoration, the City should prioritize the central-west area identified as Cluster 0.

records.text: Discussion
records.all_revision_text: Discussion

records.text: Limitations primarily arise from scope and model resolution. The analysis considers three historical earthquake scenarios, which limits generalization. The substation is taken as a whole instead of assembly of granular components. The mapping from subsation to census tract only considers the along-grid distance without detailed distribution line information. The logistics-aware restoration similation uses predefined repair times and repair crew number while not addressing the elevated congestion after the earthquake event. The derived recovery time estimations and restoration strategy rankings may vary in alternative staffing levels and transportation conditions.

records.text: Future work can expand scenario sampling and run sensitivity tests to track the influence of fragility, repair times, tract-substation assignment, and logistics inputs on time-to-50% service, robustness, hospital coverage, and equity gaps. Addtional simulation of substation dynamic allows for more penetrating focus on the sources of vulnerability. The restoration model can be strengthened with repair task scheduling optimization, power system operational simulation, and post-earthquake road-damage-adjusted travel times.

records.text: Introduction
records.all_revision_text: Introduction

records.text: The high-voltage substations and transmission lines in Southern California face serious seismic threats. When earthquakes damage the electric system, neighborhoods in the region would experience a varying range of levels and durations of impacts, as the local access to electricity depends on which substations remain functional and how quickly they can be repaired.

When earthquakes damage the electric system, neighborhoods in the region would experience a varying range of levels and durations of impacts, as the local access to electricity depends on which substations remain functional and how quickly they can be repaired.

records.text: Evaluating post-earthquake power restoration is important because electricity is essential for economic and social activities, especially in densely populated urban areas. Since the impacts of earthquakes are not spatially uniform, an evaluation framework should quantify the impacts through population-weighted recovery indicators, tract-level restoration dispersion, time to restore hospital service, equity in restoration waiting times, network criticality of affected assets, and estimates of the loss in power supply at the network and substation levels.
records.all_revision_text: Evaluating post-earthquake power restoration is important because electricity is essential for economic and social activities, especially in densely populated urban areas. Since the impacts of earthquakes are not spatially uniform, an evaluation framework should quantify the impacts through population-weighted recovery indicators, tract-level restoration dispersion, time to restore hospital service, equity in restoration waiting times, network criticality of affected assets, and estimates of the loss in power supply at the network and substation levels.

records.text: This project identifies and analyzes such unequal levels of exposure and recovery across the census tracts in the City of Los Angeles by modeling the power grid as a network of supply and demand: substations on the supply side, census tracts on the demand side, connected by tract-specific “supply weights.” We question which substations are structurally critical for tract-level power service, how selected damage scenarios propagate through that network, and how different repair priorities influence the size of the population served by restoration.

records.text: Prior studies have shown the value of modeling earthquake-driven power-system risk using scenario ground motion, fragility-based component damage, and resource-constrained restoration scheduling. This project builds on existing literature by adding power transmission centrality network analysis and tract typologies derived from PCA and k-means clustering to evaluate both system recovery and equity outcomes in Los Angeles. We build a topological transmission network, simulate substation-level shaking intensities based on three historical earthquakes with distinct spatial footprints, and use fragility functions with Monte Carlo sampling to estimate substation damage states and expected recovery times. We then translate substation disruption into tract-level outage probabilities and simulate restoration under unconstrained and logistics-aware conditions to compare prioritization strategies based on various centrality measures.

records.text: Literature Review
records.all_revision_text: Literature Review

records.text: Among the literature on modeling earthquake risks, the recent studies by Soleimani et al. (2021) and Cheng et al. (2024) introduce novel approaches to simulate scenarios realistically. Soleimani et al. develop a multihazard method to measure earthquake risk to avoid any hazard type overrepresenting the model and results. They first map each earthquake’s ground shaking, liquefaction, and surface fault rupture to create consistent hazard maps. From a large set of possible ruptures, they screen events based on their contribution to overall risk. They then use a mixed-integer linear program to select a smaller set of representative ruptures with probabilities that reproduce the full hazard distribution. This smaller set is resampled to generate the final collection of scenarios. In a case study on the City of Los Angeles, the 351 selected scenarios produce results matching the simulations based on the full rupture set, which reduces computation time while maintaining accuracy (Soleimani et al., 2021).

records.text: Moving forward, Cheng et al. (2024) simulate 351 earthquake scenarios generated by Soleimani et al. (2021), each with 12 possible damage outcomes, to model the seismic risk in the City of Los Angeles at the census tract level. They employ the HAZUS risk modeling tool developed by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) with a Direct Current (DC) load flow model to track delivered power and load shedding (the intentional limiting or closing of power supply to prevent system overloading) over a nine-period restoration timeline. Cheng et al. find that substation damage causes most of the outages, generator damage causes secondary effects, and transmission line damage makes minimal impacts. The pattern concentrates the risks of load shedding in northern and central Los Angeles tracts. In addition, Cheng et al. map system-level outages to census tracts through distance-weighted allocation. Modeling the solar plus storage adoption levels of  2030, they suggest that solar plus storage reduces early-stage load shedding, but the benefits are uneven and favor higher-income, homeowner-occupied areas (Cheng et al., 2024).

records.text: Literature that models the impacts of earthquakes on the electrical grid include the works by Shinozuka et al. (2007) and Johnson et al. (2020), both applying Monte Carlo simulation (MCS). Shinozuka et al. first calculate the Peak Ground Acceleration (PGA), a measure of earthquake intensity, at 52 receiving stations across 50 scenarios of historic earthquakes in the City of Los Angeles, such as the 1994 Northridge earthquake that made the city black out for the first time in history. Shinozuka et al. then model fragility curves, each representing the probability that a component fails given a certain PGA (Shinozuka et al., 2007). The fragility curves simulate how individual components may be damaged and generate 20 different possible outcomes of network damage for each scenario of earthquakes, reflecting a standard MCS practice of repeated trials (Radu et al., 2018). In turn, they employ power flow analysis to check how earthquakes disrupt power supply, fluctuate voltages, and disconnect transmission lines to quantify the network stability (Shinozuka et al., 2007). Similarly, Johnson et al. use fragility curves to estimate the likelihood that individual grid components fail under specific levels of seismic shaking. Their MCS then randomly samples component failure states based on each selected earthquake scenario’s fragility curve. It allows them to analyze the resulting damaged grid with a power flow solver to calculate Demand Not Served (DNS), or the loss of power supply (Johnson et al.,2020).

records.text: Studies by Çag˘nan et. al (2006) and Xu et al. (2007) cover methodologies to model the post-earthquake restoration of power systems. Çag˘nan et. al (2006) combine a seismic hazard model, a damage model developed using fragility curves and MCS, and a discrete-event restoration simulation that tracks inspections, repairs, crew travel, and resource constraints. Running multiple MCS scenarios, Çag˘nan et. al produce restoration curves that show how quickly power is restored and identify risks of long outages, uneven recovery across zones, and shortages in crews or equipment. Çag˘nan et. al show that increasing repair crews most effectively reduces long-duration outages, and they reflect considerations for equitable restoration across geographies (Çag˘nan et. al, 2006). Similarly, Xu et al. (2007) simulate post-earthquake recovery of the Los Angeles power system by scheduling inspections, damage assessments, and repairs across substations to reduce outages. They use restoration curves to track how power recovers after disruptions. The model by Xu et al. minimizes the average outage, measured by SAIDIEQ (the area above the restoration curve). They use a genetic algorithm to schedule tasks and evaluate the resulting recovery in a simulation, which reduces total outage time compared to standard approaches (Xu et al., 2007).

They use a genetic algorithm to schedule tasks and evaluate the resulting recovery in a simulation, which reduces total outage time compared to standard approaches (Xu et al., 2007).

Their model prioritizes repairs based on the amount of service restored per unit time and allocates tasks to crews to accelerate overall system restoration (Cavdaroglu et al., 2013).

records.all_revision_text: Despite the extensive literature, three methodological gaps challenge the application of existing models in real-world disaster response:

records.text: Disconnection Between Physical Damage and Functional Restoration: Existing frameworks often rely on deterministic repair tables (e.g., HAZUS) that conflate physical repair (which takes weeks) with functional restoration (which takes hours/days via grid redundancy). This "physics-only" approach systematically overestimates outage durations compared to historical records (e.g., Northridge 1994).

records.text: Methods and Results
records.all_revision_text: Methods and Results

records.text: This study establishes a multi-layered computational framework to evaluate the seismic resilience of the Los Angeles power grid, integrating critical infrastructure topology, seismological hazard modeling, and socio-demographic vulnerability. The physical network model synthesizes substation geolocation data from OpenStreetMap with high-voltage transmission geometries from the California Energy Commission (CEC) to define a topologically valid graph. To capture spatially distributed hazards, we utilize USGS ShakeMaps to assign scenario-specific Peak Ground Acceleration (PGA) intensities to each network node. We examine three historical earthquake scenarios-the 1933 Long Beach, 1971 San Fernando, and 1994 Northridge events-selected to represent diverse seismotectonic sources and distinct spatial damage footprints ranging from regional disruptions to citywide blackouts.

To capture spatially distributed hazards, we utilize USGS ShakeMaps to assign scenario-specific Peak Ground Acceleration (PGA) intensities to each network node. We examine three historical earthquake scenarios-the 1933 Long Beach, 1971 San Fernando, and 1994 Northridge events-selected to represent diverse seismotectonic sources and distinct spatial damage footprints ranging from regional disruptions to citywide blackouts.

records.text: The societal dimension of these disruptions is assessed by overlaying the physical grid onto U.S. Census Bureau tract boundaries, populated with American Community Survey (ACS) demographic data and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) scores to quantify equity in recovery. Furthermore, human mobility dynamics are incorporated using Origin-Destination (OD) trip data from Replica, enabling the estimation of "flow loss" where travel is impeded by power outages.

Furthermore, human mobility dynamics are incorporated using Origin-Destination (OD) trip data from Replica, enabling the estimation of "flow loss" where travel is impeded by power outages.

records.text: The simulation pipeline progresses through three analytical stages. First, stochastic fragility modeling maps local PGA values to discrete substation damage states via lognormal fragility functions, using Monte Carlo simulation to sample probabilistic failure modes and physical repair times. Second, network criticality analysis evaluates structural robustness using graph metrics (e.g., degree and betweenness) and impact-based measures quantifying the fragmentation of the Largest Connected Component (LCC). Finally, functional restoration is simulated under two regimes: a theoretical unconstrained baseline and a realistic, resource-constrained scheduling model involving 28 repair crews dispatched from 7 bases with explicit travel-time modeling (Los Angeles Department of Water and Power). Within this constrained environment, we evaluate the efficacy of four prioritization strategies-Random, Centrality-first, Impact-first (Population), and Hospital-first-aggregating component-level repairs into system-level recovery curves. The analysis concludes by classifying census tracts into resilience typologies using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and K-Means clustering, thereby identifying distinct vulnerability profiles based on recovery performance and socio-demographic characteristics.

records.text: Data Preparation
records.all_revision_text: Data Preparation

records.text: The foundation of the simulation is the integration of heterogeneous geospatial datasets. The physical power grid is represented by substation point inventories and high-voltage transmission line geometries synthesized from California Energy Commission (CEC) and Homeland Infrastructure Foundation-Level Data (HIFLD) sources. To characterize seismic hazards, we assign scenario-specific Peak Ground Acceleration (PGA) values to each substation by sampling spatially interpolated ShakeMap fields. Census tracts serve as the fundamental unit of analysis, represented by attributes including geometry, population, Social Vulnerability Index (SVI), National Risk Index (NRI) and hospital locations. The study area is set within the City of Los Angeles administrative boundaries.

records.text: Topological Reconstruction of the Transmission Network
records.all_revision_text: Topological Reconstruction of the Transmission Network

records.text: Transforming raw GIS geometries into a mathematically valid network graph G is a critical prerequisite for subsequent analysis. MultiLineString of Transmission lines are first broken into LineString segments, whose endpoints are snapped to the nearest substation coordinates within a spatial tolerance of 300 m using a KD-tree index. Transmission lines passing through substations without explicit vertices are split at intersection points to ensure that all substations function as active nodes within the topology. An undirected weighted MultiGraph is then constructed using the vertices in LineStrings and edges connecting every consecutive vertex. This serves as a model representation of the real transmission graph. Substations are snapped to the nearest graph node. The substation-substation distances are then calculated by Dijkstra shortest path on graph G.

records.text: The topological graph requires straight connection between each pair of directly connected substations, instead of the real geometry. A pair is considered directly adjacent only if the vertices listed in the shortest path are not associated with any other substation. An undirected edge is then constructed between directly adjacent pairs with the weight being the calculated along-grid shortest path.

records.text: Graph construction
records.all_revision_text: Graph construction

records.text: As is discussed, transmission corridors are converted into a substation-level undirected graph G=(V,E), where nodes V represent substations and edges E represent direct corridor connectivity implied by the CEC edge list. records.text: Resource-Constrained Dispatch Model
records.all_revision_text: Resource-Constrained Dispatch Model

records.text: We model post-earthquake restoration as a resource-constrained Multi-Depot Vehicle Routing and Scheduling Problem (MDVRSP). Let S be the set of all substations, and let J⊆S denote the subset classified as damaged in a given Monte Carlo realization. A finite workforce of K=28 repair crews is distributed across D=7maintenance depots. Each crew k∈{1,…,K} is anchored to a home depot d(k)∈D at initialization and executes a time-ordered sequence of repair tasks.
records.all_revision_text: We model post-earthquake restoration as a resource-constrained Multi-Depot Vehicle Routing and Scheduling Problem (MDVRSP). Let S be the set of all substations, and let J⊆S denote the subset classified as damaged in a given Monte Carlo realization. A finite workforce of K=28 repair crews is distributed across D=7maintenance depots. Each crew k∈{1,…,K} is anchored to a home depot d(k)∈D at initialization and executes a time-ordered sequence of repair tasks.

records.text: State variables. At any decision epoch, each crew is characterized by its current location (either a depot or the most recently completed substation), and its next-available time. The system state is defined by the set of remaining unrepaired damaged substations and the crew states. Each damaged substation j∈J is a single indivisible task that can be served by exactly one crew; parallel work on a single substation is not modeled.

At any decision epoch, each crew is characterized by its current location (either a depot or the most recently completed substation), and its next-available time. records.text: Travel-time coupling. Spatial frictions are modeled through a precomputed impedance matrix τ(a,b) (hours) between any two locations a,b∈D∪S. These travel times are computed from shortest paths on a routable OpenStreetMap road graph, ensuring that dispatch decisions reflect the actual topology of the Los Angeles transportation network rather than straight-line distances. The travel-time matrix is treated as fixed for a given analysis run. It does not depend on time of day or post-event road degradation unless explicitly modeled elsewhere.

records.text: Operational constraints. The formulation enforces (i) crew capacity: at most K concurrent repairs, one per crew; (ii) precedence in time: a crew cannot start a task until it has completed its prior task and traveled to the new site; and (iii) geographic feasibility: crews begin at their assigned depots and move along the road network, incurring travel time between consecutive tasks.

records.text: Because the full MDVRSP is NP-hard at realistic network scales, we do not attempt an exact optimization. Instead, we evaluate a family of policy-driven greedy heuristics within a discrete-event simulation, which allows transparent comparisons among prioritization strategies while preserving the key physical constraints.

records.text: Recovery is simulated using a logistics-aware Discrete-Event Simulation (DES) that advances time by operational events rather than fixed time steps. Two event types are sufficient to define the restoration timeline: Crew availability (decision event) occurs when a crew becomes free to accept a new assignment at time t. Repair completion (state-change event) occurs when a substation transitions to the functional state at the instant its repair finishes.

records.text: Figure 7: Correlations of Degree, Betweenness, and Impact Centralities
records.all_revision_text: Figure 7: Correlations of Degree, Betweenness, and Impact Centralities

records.text: Figure 7 reports pairwise correlations among structural centrality measures (degree, closeness, and betweenness) and two consequence-oriented measures (impact centrality and impact population). The structural metrics are moderately to strongly correlated, with degree most closely correlating with closeness (r = 0.71) and more moderate correlations between betweenness and both closeness (r = 0.59) and degree (r = 0.51). In contrast, impact centrality is largely decoupled from simple connectivity and reachability, showing near-zero correlation with degree (r = 0.07) and a weak correlation with closeness (r = 0.17), but a moderate relationship with betweenness (r = 0.59), consistent with bridge-like substations driving disproportionate consequences. Impact population is moderately correlated with impact centrality (r = 0.67) and also relates to betweenness (r = 0.51) more than to degree (r = 0.06), indicating that population exposure is better captured by network position and flow importance than by node degree alone.

records.text: The results indicate that substation importance depends on which centrality is considered. Degree centrality captures local connectivity, but a high degree does not reliably translate into systemwide consequence. Betweenness centrality highlights bridge nodes that concentrate shortest-path routing and therefore represent potential bottlenecks. Impact centrality directly reflects fragmentation risk by measuring how much network connectivity contracts when a node is removed, and its weak correlation with degree and closeness suggests that the most disruptive substations are not always the most connected or the most accessible. Taken together, these centralities imply that restoration priorities should be guided by nodes with high impact centrality and, secondarily, high betweenness centrality, rather than high degree alone.

records.text: The percolation curves in Figure 11 track the largest connected component (LCC) fraction as substations are removed. Thereafter the LCC fraction stabilizes above 0.1 until more than 40 nodes are randomly removed.

records.text: In contrast, the targeted attack (impact/λ₂-targeted) removes nodes ranked by impact centrality, so each removal is chosen to maximally reduce global connectivity. As a result, the LCC fraction falls much faster: within the first 15 targeted removals, the LCC fraction drops to roughly 0.25, long before the random case reaches comparable degradation. After this early collapse, the remaining nodes are largely in smaller components, so additional removals produce smaller changes until the LCC eventually decays toward 0 after around 35 nodes are removed. The two percolation curves indicate that the network is substantially more vulnerable to failures at a small set of high-impact substations than to the same number of random outages.

records.text: Figure 22 compares the time until 50% recovery among scenarios. In the Long Beach scenario (Figure 22a), system recovery to 50% power supply ranges from 2 to 3 hours, with the Degree-first, Betweenness-first, and Closeness-first strategies showing the fastest recovery outcomes. In the San Fernando scenario (Figure 22b), recovery speed is moderate, taking 5 to 7 hours to 50% and showing the outstanding efficiency of the Degree-first strategy. In the Northridge scenario (Figure 22c), recovery is the slowest, taking 21 to 24 hours to 50%, with Betweenness-first and Degree-first strategies showing the best outcomes. Across scenarios, Degree-first and Betweenness-first prioritizations show the most efficient restoration.

records.text: Future Work and Conclusions
records.all_revision_text: Future Work and Conclusions

records.text: This project presents a comprehensive pipeline to evaluate earthquake impacts on electric transmission-grid functionality and tract-level outcomes. A topological representation of the transmission network is constructed to support substation centrality and criticality analysis. For three earthquake scenarios, scenario-specific intensity fields are assigned to substations, fragility functions are applied to estimate probabilistic substation damage states, and a tract-substation mapping matrix propagates substation disruption into census-tract outage probabilities, producing spatially explicit impact maps. Recovery across scenarios is then simulated and compared using power-supply restoration and network-robustness metrics under both unconstrained and logistics-aware restoration conditions. The project concludes with principal component analysis (PCA) and k-means clustering to classify census tracts into resilience typologies based on simulated recovery outcomes and socio-economic attributes.
records.all_revision_text: This project presents a comprehensive pipeline to evaluate earthquake impacts on electric transmission-grid functionality and tract-level outcomes. A topological representation of the transmission network is constructed to support substation centrality and criticality analysis. For three earthquake scenarios, scenario-specific intensity fields are assigned to substations, fragility functions are applied to estimate probabilistic substation damage states, and a tract-substation mapping matrix propagates substation disruption into census-tract outage probabilities, producing spatially explicit impact maps. Recovery across scenarios is then simulated and compared using power-supply restoration and network-robustness metrics under both unconstrained and logistics-aware restoration conditions. The project concludes with principal component analysis (PCA) and k-means clustering to classify census tracts into resilience typologies based on simulated recovery outcomes and socio-economic attributes.

records.text: Overall, the City of Los Angeles power grid forms a connected, highly clustered small-world network, so restoring a relatively small set of structurally important substations can rapidly improve systemwide connectivity. However, which substations count as “important” depends on the centrality metric used (e.g., degree vs. betweenness vs. impact), and these network-based priorities do not necessarily coincide with equity-priority considerations. In our simulation of the 1933 Long Beach, the 1971 San Fernando, and the 1994 Northridge earthquake scenarios, the Northridge creates the most damage and requires the longest time for reparation. Across scenarios, prioritizing the repair of substations with high Degree Centrality or Betweenness Centrality and those serving hospitals are shown to be the most efficient strategies for the system service recovery to 50%.

In our simulation of the 1933 Long Beach, the 1971 San Fernando, and the 1994 Northridge earthquake scenarios, the Northridge creates the most damage and requires the longest time for reparation. Across scenarios, prioritizing the repair of substations with high Degree Centrality or Betweenness Centrality and those serving hospitals are shown to be the most efficient strategies for the system service recovery to 50%.

records.text: Results suggest the following three restoration schemes targeting different objectives. For efficient restoration of the power-grid network, the City should prioritize substations with high degree to reconnect large portions of the network quickly or high betweenness to protect bridge nodes that maintain global connectivity. For efficient restoration of electricity service to the population, the City should prioritize substations that serve tracts containing hospitals, paired with high-degree substations for faster restoration of connectivity, as well as high-betweenness substations to preserve cross-area connectivity and prevent the grid from splitting into isolated components. For equitable restoration, the City should prioritize the central-west area identified as Cluster 0.

records.text: The limitations of this study primarily arise from scope and model resolution. The analysis considers three historical earthquake scenarios, which limits generalization. The mapping from substation to census tract only considers the along-grid distance without detailed distribution line information. The logistics-aware restoration simulation uses predefined repair times and repair crew number while not addressing the elevated congestion after the earthquake event. The derived recovery time estimations and restoration strategy rankings may vary in alternative staffing levels and transportation conditions.

records.text: Future work can expand scenario sampling and run sensitivity tests to track the influence of fragility, repair times, tract-substation assignment, and logistics inputs on time-to-50% service, robustness, hospital coverage, and equity gaps. The restoration model can be strengthened with repair task scheduling optimization, power system operational simulation, and post-earthquake road-damage-adjusted travel times.

records.text: Existing assessments of earthquake impacts on electric infrastructure often examine physical damage, network performance, restoration operations, and community service consequences separately. Our study brings these elements together in a census-tract-scale framework for the Los Angeles metropolitan area. The framework models how scenario-based substation damage affects census-tract-level power-service recovery while accounting for network connectivity, tract–substation dependencies, repair logistics, and alternative restoration strategies.
records.all_revision_text: Existing assessments of earthquake impacts on electric infrastructure often examine physical damage, network performance, restoration operations, and community service consequences separately. Our study brings these elements together in a census-tract-scale framework for the Los Angeles metropolitan area. The framework models how scenario-based substation damage affects census-tract-level power-service recovery while accounting for network connectivity, tract–substation dependencies, repair logistics, and alternative restoration strategies.

records.text: The results show that post-earthquake power-service recovery cannot be explained by network centrality alone. Population exposure, tract–substation dependencies, crew constraints, travel logistics, and repair sequencing jointly determine the pace and spatial distribution of service restoration. Strategies prioritizing hospitals and large affected populations show stronger recovery performance than strategies based only on topological importance. The analysis also identifies census tracts where delayed modeled restoration coincides with social vulnerability, older housing stock, and elevated disaster-risk exposure.

The analysis also identifies census tracts where delayed modeled restoration coincides with social vulnerability, older housing stock, and elevated disaster-risk exposure.

records.text: Aligned with IJDRR’s multidisciplinary focus, the study offers a quantitative framework for comparing system-, population-, and critical-service-oriented restoration priorities and for identifying communities where prolonged power-service disruption may compound existing vulnerabilities.

title: From Substation Damage to Community Recovery: Tract-Level Assessment of Post-Earthquake Power-Service Restoration in Los Angeles

records.text: From Substation Damage to Community Recovery: Tract-Level Assessment of Post-Earthquake Power-Service Restoration in Los Angeles
records.all_revision_text: From Substation Damage to Community Recovery: Tract-Level Assessment of Post-Earthquake Power-Service Restoration in Los Angeles

records.text: Yinchen Yi, Yutong Li, Marta C. González
records.all_revision_text: Yinchen Yi, Yutong Li, Marta C. González

records.text: Abstract
records.all_revision_text: Abstract

records.text: Major earthquakes can extensively disrupt electric-power systems, resulting in prolonged and spatially uneven power-service losses within metropolitan regions. In metropolitan regions, post-earthquake power recovery depends not only on which transmission and substation assets are damaged, but also on how restoration resources are dispatched and which communities remain without service. This study presents a census tract-level framework for evaluating post-earthquake electric-power service disruption and recovery in the contiguous urban area of Los Angeles County. The framework reconstructs a source-gated transmission topology, simulates scenario-based substation damage using fragility functions, translates substation functionality into census-tract service availability through tract-substation dependency weights, and compares unconstrained recovery with logistics-aware restoration strategies, including rule-based priorities and Genetic Algorithm (GA)-based scheduling recommendations. Using the 2%-in-50-year seismic scenario as the primary case, the results show that network vulnerability is concentrated in a limited set of high-impact substations and that tract-level recovery is spatially uneven even before crew-dispatch constraints are introduced. Under logistics-aware restoration, strategy performance cannot be explained by network centrality alone because population exposure, tract-substation dependency, and repair sequencing jointly shape service recovery. The hospital-prioritized rule provides the fastest recovery among the tested logistics-aware strategies, while the population-impact rule provides a competitive non-optimization alternative and GA-HospitalFirst performs best among the GA-based schedules. The recovery-vulnerability typology further shows that delayed modeled restoration and social vulnerability are not perfectly aligned. A composite hotspot analysis identifies the tracts where slow recovery, social vulnerability, older housing stock, and disaster-risk exposure coincide. The proposed framework supports socio-technical risk-informed restoration planning by comparing recovery priorities and identifying communities where post-earthquake power-service delays may compound vulnerabilities and exacerbate inequities.

records.text: Introduction
records.all_revision_text: Introduction

records.text: Electric systems serve as the backbone for the normal operation of society. As key components, the functionality of substations and transmission lines is critical for the overall supply and service of electricity. When earthquakes damage the electric-power system, neighborhoods can experience different levels and durations of service disruption because local electricity access depends on which substations remain functional, how transmission connectivity is affected, and how quickly damaged assets can be restored. Post-earthquake power recovery is therefore not only a system-performance problem, but also a community-service problem, as electricity supports emergency response, healthcare operation and communication in affected areas. Recent resilience research has emphasized that infrastructure recovery should not be evaluated only through aggregate system functionality, because service losses and restoration delays are often spatially uneven and socially differentiated.

records.text: 1.1 Equity-aware infrastructure restoration
records.all_revision_text: 1.1 Equity-aware infrastructure restoration

records.text: Recent infrastructure resilience studies have increasingly shifted from system-centered performance metrics toward community-centered recovery outcomes. Logan and Guikema (2020) reframed community resilience around equitable access to essential services, emphasizing that recovery should be evaluated not only by infrastructure functionality, but also by residents’ spatially uneven access to services such as food, health care, education, water, power, sanitation, and communications. Dhakal and Zhang (2022) incorporated social equity and vulnerability into infrastructure resilience assessment by accounting for unequal distributions of functional loss and recovery time, thereby linking resilience metrics to both inequality and impacts on socially vulnerable communities. Ding et al. (2026) extended this line of work to the census-tract scale by examining the spatial-temporal dynamics of public infrastructure service inequality during hurricanes using 311 service-request data, showing that reported service requests and resolution time vary systematically across geographic exposure, social vulnerability, and disaster-risk groups. In the power-outage context, Loni and Asadi (2024) developed a data-driven index of social vulnerability to prolonged outages in California, while Lin et al. (2022) framed equity as a missing dimension in power-grid resilience and argued that recognitional, procedural, and distributional equity should be embedded into power-system planning and disaster management. Esmalian et al. (2022) further showed, through a hazard-household-infrastructure multi-agent model, that infrastructure service disruptions can impose uneven household-level hardship, highlighting the need to evaluate recovery outcomes across socially differentiated populations.

records.text: Beyond assessment, a related body of work has incorporated community characteristics into restoration planning and resource-allocation models. Chen et al. (2025a) advanced community-centered infrastructure restoration by combining population size, social vulnerability, and public facilities, such as hospitals and emergency shelters, into restoration-priority weights for interdependent power and water infrastructure recovery. Li et al. (2023) proposed a data-driven and equity-centered framework for highway restoration following flood inundation, linking damage identification, restoration scheduling, and progress monitoring while considering social vulnerability in restoration prioritization. Chen et al. (2025b) developed a human-centered infrastructure restoration framework that estimates post-disaster community demand using Bayesian updating and links demand uncertainty to restoration resource allocation for interdependent infrastructure systems. In power-grid resilience planning, Toplu-Tutay et al. (2024) incorporated equity metrics into a stochastic substation-hardening and power-flow optimization framework, approximating community-level outage impacts through census-tract-level vulnerability and well-being-loss measures.

records.text: Together, these studies show that a growing body of disaster recovery research has moved beyond purely technical system restoration and has begun to account for essential-service access and equity-aware resource allocation. These studies provide the conceptual and methodological basis for evaluating restoration outcomes by asking not only how much infrastructure functionality is restored, but also which communities regain service, when they regain it, and how recovery benefits and burdens are distributed across space.

records.section: 1.2 Substation Fragility, Repair Scheduling, Lifeline Restoration, and Critical Service Restoration
records.text: 1.2 Substation Fragility, Repair Scheduling, Lifeline Restoration, and Critical Service Restoration
records.all_revision_text: 1.2 Substation Fragility, Repair Scheduling, Lifeline Restoration, and Critical Service Restoration

records.section: 1.2 Substation Fragility, Repair Scheduling, Lifeline Restoration, and Critical Service Restoration
records.text: A parallel stream of research has developed repair-scheduling, routing, and restoration-optimization models for disrupted critical infrastructure systems. Xu et al. (2026) reviewed post-disaster repair-resource scheduling models and showed that past research has matured around restoration objectives, scheduling and routing decisions, operation constraints, uncertainty treatment, and solution algorithms. Within this stream, Li et al. (2019) developed a joint optimization model that simultaneously assigns restoration tasks to multiple teams, schedules component repairs, and routes crews among geographically distributed damaged components while evaluating recovery performance using maximal network flow and unmet demand. Loggins et al. (2019) developed the CRISIS decision-support model to schedule repairs of damaged civil infrastructure according to stakeholder-defined priorities for dependent social infrastructure services, capturing interdependencies between civil systems and critical social functions.

records.section: 1.2 Substation Fragility, Repair Scheduling, Lifeline Restoration, and Critical Service Restoration
records.text: Related work has also expanded restoration scheduling beyond purely component-based repair decisions. Shahverdi et al. (2025) formulated a decision-support model that coordinates specialized repair crews across interdependent power, water, and transportation lifelines to prioritize critical societal services such as hospitals. Shahverdi et al. (2024) further modeled personnel as “human infrastructure,” emphasizing that critical services require not only functional buildings and lifeline support but also skilled personnel who can remain in the affected area and travel to their workplaces. Recent power-restoration models have also addressed uncertainty-aware and adaptive decision-making: Jiang et al. (2025) proposed a predict-then-optimize framework that combines repair-duration uncertainty prediction with equity-constrained power restoration sequencing, and Li et al. (2026) developed a post-earthquake electricity-gas restoration framework that jointly models damage-information collection and repair-vehicle routing under partial observability.

records.section: 1.2 Substation Fragility, Repair Scheduling, Lifeline Restoration, and Critical Service Restoration
records.text: For earthquake-specific power-system recovery, prior studies have coupled seismic damage, network functionality, and restoration decisions at the system or component level. Xie et al. (2024) developed a resilience-based optimisation framework for post-earthquake power-system restoration by linking seismic-intensity attenuation, fragility-based component operational-state assessment, graph-based system functionality metrics, and recovery-path optimisation. Fu et al. (2024) advanced seismic vulnerability assessment of electrical substation systems by combining hybrid equipment fragility functions, Bayesian updating with seismic damage-survey data, and a Bayesian-network representation of substation topology and redundancy to infer system functionality and component importance. These studies provide foundations for modeling how earthquake-induced component damage affects power-system functionality and recovery priorities.

records.section: 1.2 Substation Fragility, Repair Scheduling, Lifeline Restoration, and Critical Service Restoration
records.text: Several studies are especially relevant to earthquake-induced electric-power risk and restoration within Los Angeles County. Monte Carlo-based studies have linked earthquake ground motion, component fragility, and electric transmission-network performance through power-flow analysis. Shinozuka et al. (2007) evaluated seismic disruption of the Los Angeles City power transmission network by sampling component damage under multiple earthquake scenarios and assessing resulting network performance, while Johnson et al. (2020) similarly used Monte Carlo simulation and power-flow analysis to estimate demand not served under seismic damage. Other scenario-based work has emphasized the representation of regional earthquake hazard and downstream outage consequences. Soleimani et al. (2021) developed a Los Angeles City multi-hazard earthquake scenario selection method that preserves risk estimates for ground shaking, liquefaction, and surface fault rupture while reducing computational burden. Building on these scenarios, Cheng et al. (2024) quantified census-tract-level electric-power risk in Los Angeles City by combining probabilistic earthquake and damage scenarios, HAZUS-based component damage, DC load-flow analysis, and tract-level load-shed allocation, showing that substation damage is a major driver of outage risk and that solar-plus-storage benefits may remain spatially and socially uneven.

records.section: 1.2 Substation Fragility, Repair Scheduling, Lifeline Restoration, and Critical Service Restoration
records.text: Other studies have modeled post-earthquake electric-power restoration processes in Los Angeles more directly. Çağnan et al. (2006) provided an early City of Los Angeles-specific benchmark for post-earthquake electric-power restoration by using discrete-event simulation to project hazard-driven substation damage as restoration rapidity risk. Their results showed that outage duration can vary geographically across Los Angeles Department of Water and Power (LADWP) service areas and can be shaped as much by repair-team and material bottlenecks as by initial component damage. Xu et al. (2007) further formulated a stochastic optimization model for scheduling LADWP post-earthquake inspection, damage assessment, and repair tasks, using restoration curves and outage-duration metrics to compare optimized schedules with baseline or utility-informed restoration schedules. More broadly, logistics-oriented restoration studies such as Cavdaroglu et al. (2013) show that repair sequencing, crew assignment, travel time, precedence relationships, and repair uncertainty can substantially affect infrastructure recovery trajectories.

records.section: 1.2 Substation Fragility, Repair Scheduling, Lifeline Restoration, and Critical Service Restoration
records.text: Taken together, this body of work provides the engineering and logistical foundation for modeling earthquake-induced power-system disruption and recovery. These studies have advanced power-flow-based outage assessment, substation fragility modeling, repair scheduling and logistics-aware recovery analysis. Their contributions show how damaged infrastructure components, network constraints, resource limitations, and restoration operations shape power-system recovery trajectories.

records.text: 1.3 Focus of This Study
records.all_revision_text: 1.3 Focus of This Study

records.text: Despite these advances, a specific gap remains for earthquake-induced urban power-service recovery: few studies perform a single metropolitan earthquake power-service recovery assessment that links physical damage, restoration operations, and tract-level recovery disparities. This gap limits the ability to evaluate not only how quickly the power system recovers, but also how physical damage, restoration logistics, and prioritization rules translate into uneven power-service recovery across census tracts and vulnerable communities.

records.text: Building on prior studies of earthquake-driven power-system risk, fragility-based component damage, and resource-constrained restoration scheduling, this study asks three questions:
records.all_revision_text: Building on prior studies of earthquake-driven power-system risk, fragility-based component damage, and resource-constrained restoration scheduling, this study asks three questions:

records.text: How do earthquake-induced substation damage and source-gated transmission network connectivity translate into census-tract-level power-service disruption and recovery trajectories?
records.all_revision_text: How do earthquake-induced substation damage and source-gated transmission network connectivity translate into census-tract-level power-service disruption and recovery trajectories?

records.text: How do utility yard logistics, crew constraints, and restoration prioritization strategies affect population-weighted recovery and critical-service restoration?
records.all_revision_text: How do utility yard logistics, crew constraints, and restoration prioritization strategies affect population-weighted recovery and critical-service restoration?

records.text: Which census tracts experience prolonged or vulnerability-amplified recovery, and how can these outcomes be characterized through tract-level recovery-vulnerability typologies?
records.all_revision_text: Which census tracts experience prolonged or vulnerability-amplified recovery, and how can these outcomes be characterized through tract-level recovery-vulnerability typologies?

records.text: To address these questions, this study develops a tract-level assessment of post-earthquake electric-power service disruption and recovery for the study area. The assessment couples scenario-specific seismic intensity, substation fragility, source-gated transmission/substation topology, tract-to-substation dependency mapping, damage-conditioned stochastic repair durations, road-network travel from repair-yard origins, alternative restoration-prioritization strategies, and consolidated metric-based tract typology identification. This framework builds on earthquake-induced substation damage to model power-service recovery trajectories for individual census tracts. Recovery outcomes are evaluated using tract-level service metrics, including population-weighted recovery time and vulnerability-related recovery typologies derived from social, demographic, built-environment, and simulated recovery indicators. A sensitivity analysis further examines how assumptions on crew availability, repair-time scale, Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) dependency threshold, and source-gate threshold affect absolute recovery times and strategy-ranking stability. This study combines established hazard, fragility, network-dependency, repair-logistics, and vulnerability-assessment components into a transparent workflow for evaluating earthquake-specific power-service recovery and community-level recovery disparities.

records.text: Methodology
records.all_revision_text: Methodology

records.text: Figure 1: Study Workflow. The framework consists of five core modules: (1) Topology and Dependency Construction, which builds the source-gated transmission network and tract-substation dependency mapping; (2) Seismic Damage Simulation, which estimates substation damage states using fragility functions; (3) Damage-to-Service Translation, which translates substation-level physical damage into tract-level service availability; (4) Recovery Modeling, which simulates restoration trajectories under unconstrained baselines and logistics-aware scheduling; and (5) Outputs and Interpretation, which evaluates population-weighted recovery metrics and identifies recovery-vulnerability hotspots.

records.text: Figure 1 summarizes the workflow used to evaluate post-earthquake electric-power service disruption and recovery in the study area. The workflow begins with five groups of input data: transmission lines and substations, scenario Peak Ground Acceleration (PGA) fields, roads and utility yards, hospitals, and tract-level attributes. These inputs are then processed through five analytical modules: topology and dependency construction, seismic damage simulation, damage-to-service translation, recovery modeling, and outputs interpretation. Together, the workflow converts scenario-specific substation damage into tract-level service recovery trajectories and recovery-vulnerability outcomes.

records.text: First, a transmission topology is constructed by combining substation point records with high-voltage transmission-line geometries. The resulting graph is used to represent network connectivity, identify source-connected components, and compute structural criticality measures such as degree, betweenness, and connectivity-related impact on the largest connected component. In parallel, a tract-to-substation dependency matrix is developed to allocate substation functionality to census tracts using topology-informed spatial proximity.
