The resulting graph is used to represent network connectivity, identify source-connected components, and compute structural criticality measures such as degree, betweenness, and connectivity-related impact on the largest connected component. In parallel, a tract-to-substation dependency matrix is developed to allocate substation functionality to census tracts using topology-informed spatial proximity.

records.text: Second, seismic hazard intensity is assigned to each substation from scenario PGA fields. The analysis considers three historical earthquake scenarios, the 1933 Long Beach, 1971 San Fernando, and 1994 Northridge events, together with a probabilistic 2%-in-50-year scenario. Lognormal fragility functions are then used in a Monte Carlo procedure to sample discrete substation damage states. These damage states are mapped to residual functionality levels and damage-conditioned stochastic restoration durations.

records.text: Third, substation damage is translated into tract-level service disruption through a damage-to-service propagation module. Residual substation functionality is routed through the source-gated transmission topology and combined with tract-to-substation dependency weights to estimate tract-level power-service availability.

records.text: Fourth, recovery modeling is conducted under both an unconstrained baseline and a logistics-aware restoration setting. The unconstrained baseline characterizes tract-level recovery trajectories based on damage-state restoration durations without crew-dispatch constraints. The logistics-aware restoration model incorporates utility yard origins, road-network travel times, and crew constraints. Within the constrained model, recovery outcomes are compared across rule-based prioritization strategies and Genetic Algorithm (GA)-based optimization benchmarks to evaluate how resource-constrained task sequencing affects tract-level service restoration.

records.text: Finally, recovery outcomes are interpreted using weighted recovery metrics, sensitivity analysis, and recovery-vulnerability typologies. Population- and vulnerability-weighted recovery trajectories are used to compare restoration strategies, while sensitivity analysis evaluates how major modeling assumptions affect recovery time and strategy-ranking stability. Simulated recovery indicators are then combined with social, demographic, built-environment, and hazard-related tract attributes. These features are standardized and fed into K-means clustering to identify census tracts where delayed recovery and vulnerability-related concerns coincide.

records.text: The pipeline integrates heterogeneous geospatial datasets. The physical power grid is represented using substation inventories and high-voltage transmission-line geometries obtained from the California Energy Commission (n.d.) and Homeland Infrastructure Foundation-Level Data (n.d.). Scenario-specific ground-motion fields are obtained from U.S. Geological Survey ShakeMap products (U.S. Geological Survey, n.d.). Census tract boundaries are obtained from U.S. Census Bureau TIGER/Line data (U.S. Census Bureau, n.d.-b), with demographic attributes joined from the American Community Survey (U.S. Census Bureau, n.d.-a). Social Vulnerability Index attributes are obtained from the CDC/ATSDR Social Vulnerability Index database (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention/Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry/Geospatial Research, Analysis, and Services Program, 2022), National Risk Index (NRI) attributes from the FEMA National Risk Index dataset (Federal Emergency Management Agency, n.d.), and hospital locations from California Health and Human Services open data (California Health and Human Services Agency, n.d.).

records.section: 2.1.1 Topological Reconstruction of the Transmission Network
records.text: 2.1.1 Topological Reconstruction of the Transmission Network
records.all_revision_text: 2.1.1 Topological Reconstruction of the Transmission Network

records.section: 2.1.1 Topological Reconstruction of the Transmission Network
records.text: To transform raw power grid geometries into a network graph, transmission line records are first decomposed into individual line-string components so that their vertices and segments can be processed consistently. Then, to reconcile spatial offsets between the line and substation layers, the endpoints of each line-string component are snapped to nearby substations. Endpoints within 150 m of a substation are directly assigned to the nearest substation, whereas endpoints within 150 to 300 m are assigned only when the nearest candidate is clearly distinguished from the second-nearest candidate, based on a minimum distance margin of 75 m and a nearest-to-second-nearest distance ratio not exceeding 0.75. To preserve existing line-line connectivity, when a junction vertex cluster satisfies the snapping criteria, all vertices in the cluster are moved together to the corresponding nearby substation. Nearby unresolved line endpoints were merged within a 75 m tolerance as a conservative geometry-repair step.

records.section: 2.1.1 Topological Reconstruction of the Transmission Network
records.text: Substations located near the interior of a line-string component are incorporated by splitting the line at the substation’s orthogonal projection point when the substation-to-line distance is within 10 m. These splits are subject to compatibility checks based on line ownership and voltage family, and a short connector representing the actual substation-to-line projection line is added when necessary. The processed geometries are then converted into an undirected weighted graph Gphys=(Vphys,ℰphys), by treating line-string vertices as graph nodes and consecutive vertex pairs as length-weighted edges. For efficient distance calculations, each substation is registered to the nearest node in Gphys.

records.section: 2.1.1 Topological Reconstruction of the Transmission Network
records.text: Unlike the physical weighted graph Gphys, the topological network G=(V,ℰ) is constructed by straight connections between each pair of directly connected substations. A pair is considered directly adjacent only if the vertices listed in the shortest path in Gphys are not associated with any other substation. Undirected weighted edges are constructed with the weight being the Dijkstra-computed along-grid shortest path length in Gphys. This reduced graph G preserves the connectivity relationships required for centrality, fragmentation, source-accessibility, and restoration analyses, but it is not interpreted as an electrical power-flow equivalent of the original transmission system.

records.text: 2.5.1 Resource-Constrained Dispatch Model
records.all_revision_text: 2.5.1 Resource-Constrained Dispatch Model

records.text: Post-earthquake restoration is modeled as a resource-constrained multi-depot routing and scheduling problem. The formulation enforces several operational constraints.
records.all_revision_text: Post-earthquake restoration is modeled as a resource-constrained multi-depot routing and scheduling problem. The formulation enforces several operational constraints.

records.text: First, crew capacity ensures that the number of concurrent restorations cannot exceed the number of crews. Each crew is anchored to a depot at initialization and executes a time-ordered sequence of tasks. At any decision, each crew is characterized by its current location, and its next available time. The system state is defined by the set of remaining damaged substations and the crew states. After the repair is completed, the task is marked complete, the crew’s location and next availability time are updated, and the substation is treated as restored. Let Ds⊆V denote the set of repair tasks under earthquake scenario s, C the set of repair crews, and ℬ the set of maintenance depots. Each crew c∈C is assigned a home depot b(c)∈ℬ and performs an ordered sequence of repair tasks. A restoration schedule is represented by

records.text: Third, path validity mandates crew to move along real road network graph edges using specified speed. Spatial frictions are modeled through a precomputed travel matrix τ(a,b) (hours) between any two locations a,b∈S. records.all_revision_text: 2.5.2 Rule-based Restoration Sequencing

records.text: Rule-based sequencing is primarily based on predefined priority criteria derived from substation-level network and service metrics. We evaluate seven strategies:
records.all_revision_text: Rule-based sequencing is primarily based on predefined priority criteria derived from substation-level network and service metrics. We evaluate seven strategies:

records.text: (1) Impact-first. Prioritizes structurally important substations to accelerate restoration of network connectivity. Substations are ranked by impact centrality first, betweenness centrality second, and node degree third.

records.text: (2) Betweenness-first. Prioritizes substations that serve as bridging nodes in the transmission graph. Substations are ranked by betweenness centrality first and node degree second.
records.all_revision_text: (2) Betweenness-first. Prioritizes substations that serve as bridging nodes in the transmission graph. Substations are ranked by betweenness centrality first and node degree second.

records.text: (3) Degree-first. Prioritizes substation connected to large number of other substations. Substations are ranked by node degree first and betweenness centrality second.

records.text: (4) Closeness-first. Prioritizes substations with short paths of connections to the rest of the network. Substations are ranked by closeness centrality first and node degree second.

records.text: (5) Impact-first (Population). Prioritizes substations expected to restore service to the largest number of people. Substations are ranked by population impact, computed as a node-level population-importance proxy from tract dependency weights and tract population.

records.text: The clustering is performed using the K-means algorithm, which partitions observations into K clusters based on minimizing Within Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS) (MacQueen, 1967; Lloyd, 1982). Candidate solutions are evaluated for K=1,…,10. Let WCSSK denote the inertia obtained for K clusters. The selected number of clusters, K∗, is determined using the elbow criterion (Thorndike, 1953), operationalized as the candidate point with the maximum perpendicular distance to the line segment connecting the first and last points of the WCSS curve. The variables summarized in Table 3 are used for clustering analysis. These variables encompass features representing power supply robustness, built environment characteristics, socio-demographic factors, and natural hazard risk exposure. The clustering analysis is used to identify distinct census-tract recovery-vulnerability typologies and to determine which groups exhibit the combined characteristics of delayed restoration, elevated social vulnerability, and greater disaster-risk exposure.

records.text: The network shown in Figure 2B is a reduced substation-level representation derived from the processed physical transmission graph in Figure 2A. A reduced edge is retained only when two registered substations are connected through the physical network and the intervening path contains no other registered substation or substation projection anchor. Although the reduced edges are displayed schematically as straight connections, each edge weight preserves the corresponding along-network shortest-path distance in the physical graph. The resulting connected network contains 92 nodes and 318 edges, with a mean degree of 6.91. Using along-network distance as the edge weight, the mean shortest-path distance over all node pairs is 41.4 km. This reduction preserves the adjacency and distance relationships required for the subsequent analyses of centrality, source connectivity, and restoration dynamics.

records.text: Substation importance depends on which centrality is considered. Degree centrality captures local connectivity, but a high degree does not necessarily drive system-wide consequence. Betweenness centrality highlights nodes that concentrate shortest-path routing and therefore represent transmission bottlenecks. Impact (λ2-based) centrality captures the contribution of a substation to global network fragmentation. Taken together, these centralities imply that restoration priorities should not be guided solely by substations with large number of transmission line connections.

Taken together, these centralities imply that restoration priorities should not be guided solely by substations with large number of transmission line connections.

records.text: Notably, when the power grid fragments into disconnected sub-networks, transmission lines would no longer connect the available supply to demand across those sub-networks, so power outage can persist even if some local assets remain functional. The percolation curves in Figure 2C track the network's LCC fraction as substations are removed. Under random removal, connectivity decreases gradually, with only two more pronounced drops around the 33rd and 67th node, respectively. In contrast, targeted removal takes out nodes ranked by the orders of various centrality metrics calculated on the original graph, so each removal degrades the network structure more than the random counterpart. Within the first 35 degree-targeted removals, the LCC fraction drops to below 0.2, long before the random case reaches comparable degradation. This indicates that the LCC decomposes much faster under targeted removal, reflecting the concentrated impact on network connectivity from a small group of high-importance substations.

records.text: This result indicates that the source-gated transmission topology is not uniformly vulnerable. Network vulnerability is concentrated in a small group of substations whose disruption can fragment the transmission network more rapidly than random outages. This topological concentration provides the structural basis for later restoration-strategy comparisons, because repairing highly connected or high-impact substations can influence not only local service restoration but also the source connectivity of network components.

records.section: 3.2 Unconstrained baseline recovery is spatially uneven across census tracts
records.text: The unconstrained baseline represents the recovery condition before crew-routing and repair-dispatch constraints are imposed. As shown in Figure 3A, tract-level T80 ranges from 35.8 to 45.8 h under the 2%-in-50-year scenario, with a large share of census tracts clustered near 43.25 h. The corresponding spatial distribution in Figure 3B shows that the longest T80 values are concentrated in the northwestern portion of the study area. These results indicate that tract-level recovery is spatially uneven even before logistics-aware crew scheduling is introduced. The variation is generated by the combined effects of spatially heterogeneous substation damage, source-gated transmission connectivity, and tract-substation dependency structure. The unconstrained baseline therefore provides a reference condition for evaluating how utility yard travel, crew constraints, and restoration-prioritization strategies further reshape recovery outcomes in logistics-aware simulations.

records.section: 3.3 Logistics-aware restoration strategies produce different population- and vulnerability-weighted recovery outcomes
records.text: Two groups of strategies are considered for logistics-aware recovery: Rule-based and GA optimization. The essence of the recovery process is the order of crew tasks and assignments. This eventually translates to a sequence of substations that need to be restored. Rule-based strategies rank substations on several priority metrics that evaluate network importance and population/hospital mapping to arrive at the sequence. A correlation matrix among topological centrality, impact centrality, and population impact metrics is provided in Figure S4. GA operates on the same restoration sequence, with the difference being that the sequence goes through evolution by means of Genetic Algorithm to maximize the schedule fitness function. As a core aspect of the logistics-aware restoration, the travel time matrix between substations is visualized in Figure S6, which serves as the temporal basis for inter-substation crew scheduling.

records.section: 3.4 Recovery-vulnerability typologies identify where delayed restoration and social vulnerability coincide
records.text: Figure S9 is the elbow plot supplying rationale behind the selection of the number of clusters, which is chosen to be five according to the criterion mentioned in the Methodology section. Figure 6 summarizes five recovery-vulnerability typologies identified across 2,291 census tracts. Cluster 1 (n=591) exhibits approximately average modeled recovery, relatively low population density and social vulnerability, and comparatively high building-value exposure. Cluster 2 (n=198) has the fastest mean recovery and is distinguished by substantially higher grid-impact centrality, indicating favorable recovery associated with dependence on structurally influential substations. Cluster 3 (n=850) combines relatively fast recovery with high population density, elevated social vulnerability, older housing stock, and lower building-value exposure. Cluster 4 (n=57) has the slowest modeled recovery despite below-average social vulnerability and disaster-risk scores, indicating that delayed service restoration is not determined by socioeconomic vulnerability alone. Cluster 5 (n=595) combines slower recovery with high population density, elevated social vulnerability, older housing stock, and high dependency-weighted degree and betweenness.

records.text: The following hotspot analysis complements the cluster typology by highlighting the locations where infrastructure recovery challenges and vulnerability-related concerns coincide most strongly. Designated as recovery-vulnerability hotspots, the ten tracts with the highest composite score highlight the locations where delayed modeled service restoration overlaps with higher social vulnerability, older housing stock, and greater natural-hazard risk. They are concentrated mainly in Cluster 5, with additional cases in Clusters 1 and 3, as shown in Figures 6-C and 6D. The pattern provides a basis for equity-informed, targeted restoration planning.

records.text: 3.5 Sensitivity Analysis
records.all_revision_text: 3.5 Sensitivity Analysis

records.text: The sensitivity analysis isolates the impact of key modeling assumptions on the baseline results. The tested ranges are grouped into two categories, namely restoration-related assumptions and topology-related assumptions. The restoration-related assumptions include crew availability and restoration time scaling, which directly affect repair capacity and damage-conditioned restoration duration. The topology-related assumptions include the IDW dependency threshold and source-gate threshold, which affect tract-substation dependency mapping and source-gated network accessibility.
records.all_revision_text: The sensitivity analysis isolates the impact of key modeling assumptions on the baseline results. The tested ranges are grouped into two categories, namely restoration-related assumptions and topology-related assumptions. The restoration-related assumptions include crew availability and restoration time scaling, which directly affect repair capacity and damage-conditioned restoration duration. The topology-related assumptions include the IDW dependency threshold and source-gate threshold, which affect tract-substation dependency mapping and source-gated network accessibility.

records.text: Figure 7 and Table 5 summarize the sensitivity of population-weighted recovery time T80pop to restoration-related and topology-related assumptions under the 2%-in-50-year scenario. The results show that population-weighted recovery milestones are primarily controlled by restoration-related assumptions. Crew availability produces the largest within-strategy change in T80pop, with a maximum shift of 49.50 h across the tested range. This reflects the substantial effect of crew capacity on parallel restoration execution. Restoration-time scaling produces a comparable maximum shift of 45.10 h, because it directly stretches or compresses the duration of damage-conditioned restoration tasks across the system. By contrast, topology-related parameters have smaller effects on aggregate T80pop. Varying the IDW dependency threshold changes how tract demand is distributed across substations, but its maximum effect on aggregate T80pop is 2.20 h. This suggests that the population-weighted recovery milestone is relatively insensitive to moderate changes in weak tract-substation links. Details about its influence on tract-substation dependency concentration can be found in Figure S12. The source-gate threshold has a larger but still subtle effect, with a maximum T80pop change of 6.00 h. This threshold affects which partially functional substations are allowed to participate in source-connected service propagation, but within the tested range it does not substantially alter the leading group of restoration strategies.

records.text: The sensitivity results also distinguish recovery-time uncertainty from strategy-ranking stability. Restoration-time scaling, IDW threshold, and source-gate threshold largely preserve the baseline strategy ranking within the tested ranges, with Spearman rank correlations of 0.99-1.00, 0.98-1.00, and 0.95-1.00, respectively. Crew availability is less rank-stable, with Spearman rank correlation ranging from 0.23 to 1.00. This indicates that crew scarcity and crew abundance can change relative strategy performance by altering the importance of repair sequencing, yard-to-task travel, and the spatial distribution of damaged substations. Rank stability measured using Spearman’s rank correlation of restoration strategies is portrayed in Figure S13.

records.text: Contextual Comparsion
records.all_revision_text: Contextual Comparsion

records.text: Because a probabilistic Los Angeles earthquake restoration scenario cannot be directly validated against observations, the modeled Northridge scenario is compared with historical Northridge restoration evidence as a contextual scale check. Çağnan et al. (2006), citing LADWP’s post-Northridge restoration record, reported that approximately 50%, 75%, 90%, 95%, and 100% of LADWP utility customers were restored within 7, 11, 19, 26, and 168 h, respectively. The present modeled Northridge scenario gives a population-weighted T80 of 14.25 h for the unconstrained baseline and 14.55-15.25 h across logistics-aware restoration strategies. Since the historical record does not directly report T80, linear interpolation between the reported 75% and 90% customer-restoration milestones gives an approximate historical value of 13.7 h. The modeled values are therefore close to the historical partial-restoration scale.

The present modeled Northridge scenario gives a population-weighted T80 of 14.25 h for the unconstrained baseline and 14.55-15.25 h across logistics-aware restoration strategies. Since the historical record does not directly report T80, linear interpolation between the reported 75% and 90% customer-restoration milestones gives an approximate historical value of 13.7 h. The modeled values are therefore close to the historical partial-restoration scale.

records.text: The comparison also shows that the model should not be treated as a replay of the 1994 event. The modeled Northridge T50 is shorter than the historical 50% customer-restoration milestone, while the modeled T90 and T95 are longer. This mismatch is expected because the present framework does not model distribution feeders, customer-level switching, or utility emergency operating records directly. Instead, it evaluates a controlled source-gated transmission service proxy. The main value of the comparison is therefore confirmation that the modeled partial-restoration scale is not inconsistent with the historical Northridge restoration record.

records.text: The mechanisms underlying the modeled Northridge scenario are also consistent with prior Los Angeles restoration modeling. Çağnan et al. (2006) found that Los Angeles residents may experience earthquake-induced power outages lasting up to about 10 days, that rapidity risk varies geographically, and that restoration can be constrained by repair materials and restoration-process limitations. Cheng et al. (2024) further showed that substation damage is the key driver of census-tract-level load-shed risk in Los Angeles, while Xu et al. (2007) treated post-earthquake LADWP restoration as a scheduling problem intended to reduce average customer outage time. The present study extends these prior findings by translating substation damage into time-dependent tract-level service recovery and by evaluating how source-gated topology, tract-substation dependency, utility yard travel, crew constraints, and restoration prioritization rules reshape recovery outcomes. The tested prioritization rules show a trade-off between optimizing overall network connectivity and minimizing the immediate impact of power outages on the population. While the network centrality-based rules allow for prompt reconstruction of the physical grid, the rules informed by tract characteristics perform better in shortening the outage duration for highly populated and vulnerable tracts.

records.text: Future Work
records.all_revision_text: Future Work

records.text: The present framework is intended as a transparent, scenario-based decision-support assessment for comparing how hazard, network dependency, repair logistics, and prioritization assumptions shape tract-level recovery outcomes. Future work can extend the present framework in several directions. First, the tract-level service representation can be refined by incorporating distribution-network topology and utility customer-feeder connection data when such data become available. This would allow transmission- and substation-level service proxies to be linked more directly to feeder-level outage and restoration patterns. Second, the tract-to-substation dependency model can be further improved by integrating utility service-territory information, feeder maps, or empirical outage records, which would reduce reliance on spatial proximity and topology-informed dependency assumptions.
records.all_revision_text: The present framework is intended as a transparent, scenario-based decision-support assessment for comparing how hazard, network dependency, repair logistics, and prioritization assumptions shape tract-level recovery outcomes. Future work can extend the present framework in several directions. First, the tract-level service representation can be refined by incorporating distribution-network topology and utility customer-feeder connection data when such data become available. This would allow transmission- and substation-level service proxies to be linked more directly to feeder-level outage and restoration patterns. Second, the tract-to-substation dependency model can be further improved by integrating utility service-territory information, feeder maps, or empirical outage records, which would reduce reliance on spatial proximity and topology-informed dependency assumptions.

records.text: The restoration component can also be expanded as more operational data become available. Future studies could calibrate damage-conditioned restoration durations using utility repair records, field inspection logs, or post-event restoration data. Road-network travel modeling could also be enhanced by incorporating post-earthquake bridge damage, road closures, congestion, emergency access restrictions, and time-varying travel conditions. In addition, the  restoration priority rules used here can be extended toward more realistic operational decision models that account for utility-specific crew dispatch protocols, material availability, mutual-aid coordination, and real-time damage information.

records.text: Further extensions can also strengthen the community-outcome interpretation. The recovery-vulnerability typology developed in this study provides a descriptive classification of recurring recovery profiles, and future work could examine the causal mechanisms linking infrastructure dependency, social vulnerability, and delayed recovery. Hospital-service restoration can also be refined by incorporating facility-level backup power, water supply, staffing, patient capacity, and road accessibility, allowing future assessments to move from infrastructure-service access toward a more comprehensive representation of hospital operational functionality.

records.text: Conclusion
records.all_revision_text: Conclusion

records.text: This study presents an integrated tract-level assessment framework for post-earthquake electric-power service recovery in the contiguous urban areas of Los Angeles County. By linking seismic damage to substation assets, source-gated transmission network connectivity, tract-substation service dependency, utility-yard and crew constraints, restoration-strategy comparison, and recovery-vulnerability typologies, the framework connects physical infrastructure disruption with community-level recovery outcomes. The analysis evaluates how restoration decisions shape recovery trajectories and, under one representative strategy, assesses how uneven recovery service availability and socio-economic characteristics interact across census tracts, identifying areas where delayed restoration overlaps with higher social vulnerability and disaster-risk exposure.
records.all_revision_text: This study presents an integrated tract-level assessment framework for post-earthquake electric-power service recovery in the contiguous urban areas of Los Angeles County. By linking seismic damage to substation assets, source-gated transmission network connectivity, tract-substation service dependency, utility-yard and crew constraints, restoration-strategy comparison, and recovery-vulnerability typologies, the framework connects physical infrastructure disruption with community-level recovery outcomes. The analysis evaluates how restoration decisions shape recovery trajectories and, under one representative strategy, assesses how uneven recovery service availability and socio-economic characteristics interact across census tracts, identifying areas where delayed restoration overlaps with higher social vulnerability and disaster-risk exposure.

records.text: The results show that post-earthquake electric-power service recovery in the study area is shaped by the interaction of network topology, tract-level dependency, repair logistics, and social vulnerability. The source-gated topology concentrates network vulnerability in a limited set of high-impact substations, while the unconstrained baseline shows that tract-level recovery already varies spatially before crew-dispatch constraints are introduced. Under logistics-aware restoration, utility yard locations, crew availability, travel time, and prioritization rules further differentiate recovery outcomes.
records.all_revision_text: The results show that post-earthquake electric-power service recovery in the study area is shaped by the interaction of network topology, tract-level dependency, repair logistics, and social vulnerability. The source-gated topology concentrates network vulnerability in a limited set of high-impact substations, while the unconstrained baseline shows that tract-level recovery already varies spatially before crew-dispatch constraints are introduced. Under logistics-aware restoration, utility yard locations, crew availability, travel time, and prioritization rules further differentiate recovery outcomes.

records.text: The strategy comparison indicates that restoration priorities should be selected according to the planning objective. Network centrality measures are useful for identifying substations that are structurally important to transmission-network connectivity, but service-oriented strategies, especially those based on population impact and hospital-related priority, minimize the durations of service outages. GA-based strategies further show that milestone recovery, cumulative recovery, and complete recovery can favor different restoration schedules and should therefore serve as complementary performance metrics. Under the 2%-in-50-year scenario, the hospital-first rule achieves the earliest population- and SVI-weighted T80 and the highest corresponding AUC values among the logistics-aware strategies.

GA-based strategies further show that milestone recovery, cumulative recovery, and complete recovery can favor different restoration schedules and should therefore serve as complementary performance metrics. Under the 2%-in-50-year scenario, the hospital-first rule achieves the earliest population- and SVI-weighted T80 and the highest corresponding AUC values among the logistics-aware strategies.

records.text: The recovery-vulnerability typology provides an additional community-level interpretation. The clustering results show that delayed restoration and social vulnerability are not perfectly aligned. Some socially vulnerable tracts recover relatively quickly in the modeled service network, while some slower-recovery tracts are not among the most socially vulnerable. Therefore, the most policy-relevant recovery-equity concern is concentrated in tracts where delayed restoration overlaps with higher social vulnerability, older housing stock, and greater disaster-risk exposure. The top recovery-vulnerability hotspots provide a more targeted screening output than either recovery time or social vulnerability alone.

records.text: These findings address the study’s three core research questions. First, earthquake-induced substation damage translates to tract-level disruption via the combined effects of spatially varying ground motion, source-gated transmission network connectivity, and tract-substation dependency, causing spatially uneven outages and differentiated layers of service importance before repair logistics are considered. Second, utility-yard logistics, crew constraints, travel times, and restoration priorities materially affect recovery. In the primary scenario, service-oriented prioritization strategies, especially hospital-oriented choices, outperform network-centrality rules in restoring power services to populations and critical hospital facilities. Finally, clustering typologies and hotspots reveal that prolonged, vulnerability-amplified recovery occurs in hotspot tracts around central Los Angeles County where delayed infrastructure restoration overlaps directly with existing socioeconomic and disaster-risk burdens.

1
From Substation Damage to Community Recovery: Tract-Level
Assessment of Post-Earthquake Power-Service Restoration in
Los Angeles
Yinchen Yi, Yutong Li, Marta C. González

2
Abstract
Major earthquakes can extensively disrupt electric-power systems, resulting in prolonged and
spatially uneven power-service losses within metropolitan regions. In metropolitan regions, post-
earthquake power recovery depends not only on which transmission and substation assets are
damaged, but also on how restoration resources are dispatched and which communities remain
without service. This study presents a census tract-level framework for evaluating post-
earthquake electric-power service disruption and recovery in the contiguous urban area of Los
Angeles County. The framework reconstructs a source-gated transmission topology, simulates
scenario-based substation damage using fragility functions, translates substation functionality
into census-tract service availability through tract-substation dependency weights, and
compares unconstrained recovery with logistics-aware restoration strategies, including rule-
based priorities and Genetic Algorithm (GA)-based scheduling recommendations. Using the 2%-
in-50-year seismic scenario as the primary case, the results show that network vulnerability is
concentrated in a limited set of high-impact substations and that tract-level recovery is spatially
uneven even before crew-dispatch constraints are introduced. Under logistics-aware restoration,
strategy performance cannot be explained by network centrality alone because population
exposure, tract-substation dependency, and repair sequencing jointly shape service recovery.
The hospital-prioritized rule provides the fastest recovery among the tested logistics-aware
strategies, while the population-impact rule provides a competitive non-optimization alternative
and GA-HospitalFirst performs best among the GA-based schedules. The recovery-vulnerability
typology further shows that delayed modeled restoration and social vulnerability are not
perfectly aligned. A composite hotspot analysis identifies the tracts where slow recovery, social
vulnerability, older housing stock, and disaster-risk exposure coincide. The proposed framework
supports socio-technical risk-informed restoration planning by comparing recovery priorities and
identifying communities where post-earthquake power-service delays may compound
vulnerabilities and exacerbate inequities.

3
Keywords
Post-earthquake recovery; Electric power grid; Critical infrastructure resilience; Substation
fragility; Repair-resource scheduling; Census tract service disruption; Social vulnerability;
Disaster equity

5
1. Introduction
Electric systems serve as the backbone for the normal operation of society. As key components,
the functionality of substations and transmission lines is critical for the overall supply and
service of electricity. When earthquakes damage the electric-power system, neighborhoods can
experience different levels and durations of service disruption because local electricity access
depends on which substations remain functional, how transmission connectivity is affected, and
how quickly damaged assets can be restored. Post-earthquake power recovery is therefore not
only a system-performance problem, but also a community-service problem, as electricity
supports emergency response, healthcare operation and communication in affected areas.
Recent resilience research has emphasized that infrastructure recovery should not be evaluated
only through aggregate system functionality, because service losses and restoration delays are
often spatially uneven and socially differentiated.
1.1 Equity-aware infrastructure restoration
Recent infrastructure resilience studies have increasingly shifted from system-centered
performance metrics toward community-centered recovery outcomes. Logan and Guikema
(2020) reframed community resilience around equitable access to essential services,
emphasizing that recovery should be evaluated not only by infrastructure functionality, but also
by residents’ spatially uneven access to services such as food, health care, education, water,
power, sanitation, and communications. Dhakal and Zhang (2022) incorporated social equity
and vulnerability into infrastructure resilience assessment by accounting for unequal
distributions of functional loss and recovery time, thereby linking resilience metrics to both
inequality and impacts on socially vulnerable communities. Ding et al. (2026) extended this line
of work to the census-tract scale by examining the spatial-temporal dynamics of public
infrastructure service inequality during hurricanes using 311 service-request data, showing that
reported service requests and resolution time vary systematically across geographic exposure,
social vulnerability, and disaster-risk groups. In the power-outage context, Loni and Asadi (2024)
developed a data-driven index of social vulnerability to prolonged outages in California, while
Lin et al. (2022) framed equity as a missing dimension in power-grid resilience and argued that
recognitional, procedural, and distributional equity should be embedded into power-system
planning and disaster management. Esmalian et al. (2022) further showed, through a hazard-
household-infrastructure multi-agent model, that infrastructure service disruptions can impose
uneven household-level hardship, highlighting the need to evaluate recovery outcomes across
socially differentiated populations.
Beyond assessment, a related body of work has incorporated community characteristics into
restoration planning and resource-allocation models. Chen et al. (2025a) advanced community-
centered infrastructure restoration by combining population size, social vulnerability, and public
facilities, such as hospitals and emergency shelters, into restoration-priority weights for
interdependent power and water infrastructure recovery. Li et al. (2023) proposed a data-driven
and equity-centered framework for highway restoration following flood inundation, linking

6
damage identification, restoration scheduling, and progress monitoring while considering social
vulnerability in restoration prioritization. Chen et al. (2025b) developed a human-centered
infrastructure restoration framework that estimates post-disaster community demand using
Bayesian updating and links demand uncertainty to restoration resource allocation for
interdependent infrastructure systems. In power-grid resilience planning, Toplu-Tutay et al.
(2024) incorporated equity metrics into a stochastic substation-hardening and power-flow
optimization framework, approximating community-level outage impacts through census-tract-
level vulnerability and well-being-loss measures.
Together, these studies show that a growing body of disaster recovery research has moved
beyond purely technical system restoration and has begun to account for essential-service
access and equity-aware resource allocation. These studies provide the conceptual and
methodological basis for evaluating restoration outcomes by asking not only how much
infrastructure functionality is restored, but also which communities regain service, when they
regain it, and how recovery benefits and burdens are distributed across space.
1.2 Substation Fragility, Repair Scheduling, Lifeline Restoration, and
Critical Service Restoration
A parallel stream of research has developed repair-scheduling, routing, and restoration-
optimization models for disrupted critical infrastructure systems. Xu et al. (2026) reviewed post-
disaster repair-resource scheduling models and showed that past research has matured around
restoration objectives, scheduling and routing decisions, operation constraints, uncertainty
treatment, and solution algorithms. Within this stream, Li et al. (2019) developed a joint
optimization model that simultaneously assigns restoration tasks to multiple teams, schedules
component repairs, and routes crews among geographically distributed damaged components
while evaluating recovery performance using maximal network flow and unmet demand.
Loggins et al. (2019) developed the CRISIS decision-support model to schedule repairs of
damaged civil infrastructure according to stakeholder-defined priorities for dependent social
infrastructure services, capturing interdependencies between civil systems and critical social
functions.
Related work has also expanded restoration scheduling beyond purely component-based repair
decisions. Shahverdi et al. (2025) formulated a decision-support model that coordinates
specialized repair crews across interdependent power, water, and transportation lifelines to
prioritize critical societal services such as hospitals. Shahverdi et al. (2024) further modeled
personnel as “human infrastructure,” emphasizing that critical services require not only
functional buildings and lifeline support but also skilled personnel who can remain in the
affected area and travel to their workplaces. Recent power-restoration models have also
addressed uncertainty-aware and adaptive decision-making: Jiang et al. (2025) proposed a
predict-then-optimize framework that combines repair-duration uncertainty prediction with
equity-constrained power restoration sequencing, and Li et al. (2026) developed a post-
earthquake electricity-gas restoration framework that jointly models damage-information
collection and repair-vehicle routing under partial observability.

7
For earthquake-specific power-system recovery, prior studies have coupled seismic damage,
network functionality, and restoration decisions at the system or component level. Xie et al.
(2024) developed a resilience-based optimisation framework for post-earthquake power-system
restoration by linking seismic-intensity attenuation, fragility-based component operational-state
assessment, graph-based system functionality metrics, and recovery-path optimisation. Fu et al.
(2024) advanced seismic vulnerability assessment of electrical substation systems by
combining hybrid equipment fragility functions, Bayesian updating with seismic damage-survey
data, and a Bayesian-network representation of substation topology and redundancy to infer
system functionality and component importance. These studies provide foundations for
modeling how earthquake-induced component damage affects power-system functionality and
recovery priorities.
Several studies are especially relevant to earthquake-induced electric-power risk and
restoration within Los Angeles County. Monte Carlo-based studies have linked earthquake
ground motion, component fragility, and electric transmission-network performance through
power-flow analysis. Shinozuka et al. (2007) evaluated seismic disruption of the Los Angeles
City power transmission network by sampling component damage under multiple earthquake
scenarios and assessing resulting network performance, while Johnson et al. (2020) similarly
used Monte Carlo simulation and power-flow analysis to estimate demand not served under
seismic damage. Other scenario-based work has emphasized the representation of regional
earthquake hazard and downstream outage consequences. Soleimani et al. (2021) developed a
Los Angeles City multi-hazard earthquake scenario selection method that preserves risk
estimates for ground shaking, liquefaction, and surface fault rupture while reducing
computational burden. Building on these scenarios, Cheng et al. (2024) quantified census-tract-
level electric-power risk in Los Angeles City by combining probabilistic earthquake and damage
scenarios, HAZUS-based component damage, DC load-flow analysis, and tract-level load-shed
allocation, showing that substation damage is a major driver of outage risk and that solar-plus-
storage benefits may remain spatially and socially uneven.
Other studies have modeled post-earthquake electric-power restoration processes in Los
Angeles more directly. Çağnan et al. (2006) provided an early City of Los Angeles-specific
benchmark for post-earthquake electric-power restoration by using discrete-event simulation to
project hazard-driven substation damage as restoration rapidity risk. Their results showed that
outage duration can vary geographically across Los Angeles Department of Water and Power
(LADWP) service areas and can be shaped as much by repair-team and material bottlenecks as
by initial component damage. Xu et al. (2007) further formulated a stochastic optimization model
for scheduling LADWP post-earthquake inspection, damage assessment, and repair tasks,
using restoration curves and outage-duration metrics to compare optimized schedules with
baseline or utility-informed restoration schedules. More broadly, logistics-oriented restoration
studies such as Cavdaroglu et al. (2013) show that repair sequencing, crew assignment, travel
time, precedence relationships, and repair uncertainty can substantially affect infrastructure
recovery trajectories.

8
Taken together, this body of work provides the engineering and logistical foundation for
modeling earthquake-induced power-system disruption and recovery. These studies have
advanced power-flow-based outage assessment, substation fragility modeling, repair scheduling
and logistics-aware recovery analysis. Their contributions show how damaged infrastructure
components, network constraints, resource limitations, and restoration operations shape power-
system recovery trajectories.
1.3 Focus of This Study
Despite these advances, a specific gap remains for earthquake-induced urban power-service
recovery: few studies perform a single metropolitan earthquake power-service recovery
assessment that links physical damage, restoration operations, and tract-level recovery
disparities. This gap limits the ability to evaluate not only how quickly the power system
recovers, but also how physical damage, restoration logistics, and prioritization rules translate
into uneven power-service recovery across census tracts and vulnerable communities.
Building on prior studies of earthquake-driven power-system risk, fragility-based component
damage, and resource-constrained restoration scheduling, this study asks three questions:
 How do earthquake-induced substation damage and source-gated transmission network
connectivity translate into census-tract-level power-service disruption and recovery
trajectories?
 How do utility yard logistics, crew constraints, and restoration prioritization strategies affect
population-weighted recovery and critical-service restoration?
 Which census tracts experience prolonged or vulnerability-amplified recovery, and how can
these outcomes be characterized through tract-level recovery-vulnerability typologies?
To address these questions, this study develops a tract-level assessment of post-earthquake
electric-power service disruption and recovery for the study area. The assessment couples
scenario-specific seismic intensity, substation fragility, source-gated transmission/substation
topology, tract-to-substation dependency mapping, damage-conditioned stochastic repair
durations, road-network travel from repair-yard origins, alternative restoration-prioritization
strategies, and consolidated metric-based tract typology identification. This framework builds on
earthquake-induced substation damage to model power-service recovery trajectories for
individual census tracts. Recovery outcomes are evaluated using tract-level service metrics,
including population-weighted recovery time and vulnerability-related recovery typologies
derived from social, demographic, built-environment, and simulated recovery indicators. A
sensitivity analysis further examines how assumptions on crew availability, repair-time scale,
Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) dependency threshold, and source-gate threshold affect
absolute recovery times and strategy-ranking stability. This study combines established hazard,
fragility, network-dependency, repair-logistics, and vulnerability-assessment components into a
transparent workflow for evaluating earthquake-specific power-service recovery and community-
level recovery disparities.

9
2. Methodology
Figure 1: Study Workflow. The framework consists of five core modules: (1) Topology and
Dependency Construction, which builds the source-gated transmission network and tract-
substation dependency mapping; (2) Seismic Damage Simulation, which estimates substation
damage states using fragility functions; (3) Damage-to-Service Translation, which translates
substation-level physical damage into tract-level service availability; (4) Recovery Modeling,
which simulates restoration trajectories under unconstrained baselines and logistics-aware
scheduling; and (5) Outputs and Interpretation, which evaluates population-weighted recovery
metrics and identifies recovery-vulnerability hotspots.
Figure 1 summarizes the workflow used to evaluate post-earthquake electric-power service
disruption and recovery in the study area. The workflow begins with five groups of input data:
transmission lines and substations, scenario Peak Ground Acceleration (PGA) fields, roads and
utility yards, hospitals, and tract-level attributes. These inputs are then processed through five
analytical modules: topology and dependency construction, seismic damage simulation,
damage-to-service translation, recovery modeling, and outputs interpretation. Together, the
workflow converts scenario-specific substation damage into tract-level service recovery
trajectories and recovery-vulnerability outcomes.
First, a transmission topology is constructed by combining substation point records with high-
voltage transmission-line geometries. The resulting graph is used to represent network
connectivity, identify source-connected components, and compute structural criticality measures
such as degree, betweenness, and connectivity-related impact on the largest connected

10
component. In parallel, a tract-to-substation dependency matrix is developed to allocate
substation functionality to census tracts using topology-informed spatial proximity.
Second, seismic hazard intensity is assigned to each substation from scenario PGA fields. The
analysis considers three historical earthquake scenarios, the 1933 Long Beach, 1971 San
Fernando, and 1994 Northridge events, together with a probabilistic 2%-in-50-year scenario.
Lognormal fragility functions are then used in a Monte Carlo procedure to sample discrete
substation damage states. These damage states are mapped to residual functionality levels and
damage-conditioned stochastic restoration durations.
Third, substation damage is translated into tract-level service disruption through a damage-to-
service propagation module. Residual substation functionality is routed through the source-
gated transmission topology and combined with tract-to-substation dependency weights to
estimate tract-level power-service availability.
Fourth, recovery modeling is conducted under both an unconstrained baseline and a logistics-
aware restoration setting. The unconstrained baseline characterizes tract-level recovery
trajectories based on damage-state restoration durations without crew-dispatch constraints. The
logistics-aware restoration model incorporates utility yard origins, road-network travel times, and
crew constraints. Within the constrained model, recovery outcomes are compared across rule-
based prioritization strategies and Genetic Algorithm (GA)-based optimization benchmarks to
evaluate how resource-constrained task sequencing affects tract-level service restoration.
Finally, recovery outcomes are interpreted using weighted recovery metrics, sensitivity analysis,
and recovery-vulnerability typologies. Population- and vulnerability-weighted recovery
trajectories are used to compare restoration strategies, while sensitivity analysis evaluates how
major modeling assumptions affect recovery time and strategy-ranking stability. Simulated
recovery indicators are then combined with social, demographic, built-environment, and hazard-
related tract attributes. These features are standardized and fed into K-means clustering to
identify census tracts where delayed recovery and vulnerability-related concerns coincide.
The pipeline integrates heterogeneous geospatial datasets. The physical power grid is
represented using substation inventories and high-voltage transmission-line geometries
obtained from the California Energy Commission (n.d.) and Homeland Infrastructure
Foundation-Level Data (n.d.). Scenario-specific ground-motion fields are obtained from U.S.
Geological Survey ShakeMap products (U.S. Geological Survey, n.d.). Census tract boundaries
are obtained from U.S. Census Bureau TIGER/Line data (U.S. Census Bureau, n.d.-b), with
demographic attributes joined from the American Community Survey (U.S. Census Bureau,
n.d.-a). Social Vulnerability Index attributes are obtained from the CDC/ATSDR Social
Vulnerability Index database (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention/Agency for Toxic
Substances and Disease Registry/Geospatial Research, Analysis, and Services Program, 2022),
National Risk Index (NRI) attributes from the FEMA National Risk Index dataset (Federal
Emergency Management Agency, n.d.), and hospital locations from California Health and
Human Services open data (California Health and Human Services Agency, n.d.).

11
The study area covers the contiguous urbanized portion of Los Angeles County south of the
San Gabriel Mountains, including the Los Angeles Basin, the San Fernando Valley, the San
Gabriel Valley, and the Long Beach-Harbor area. This region represents the county’ s primary
continuous urban corridor, where dense population, critical facilities, and major electric-power
infrastructure are concentrated across connected basin, valley, and coastal-plain settings.

2.1 Topological Network & Weight Matrix Construction
2.1.1 Topological Reconstruction of the Transmission Network
To transform raw power grid geometries into a network graph, transmission line records are first
decomposed into individual line-string components so that their vertices and segments can be
processed consistently. Then, to reconcile spatial offsets between the line and substation layers,
the endpoints of each line-string component are snapped to nearby substations. Endpoints
within 150 m of a substation are directly assigned to the nearest substation, whereas endpoints
within 150 to 300 m are assigned only when the nearest candidate is clearly distinguished from
the second-nearest candidate, based on a minimum distance margin of 75 m and a nearest-to-
second-nearest distance ratio not exceeding 0.75. To preserve existing line-line connectivity,
when a junction vertex cluster satisfies the snapping criteria, all vertices in the cluster are
moved together to the corresponding nearby substation. Nearby unresolved line endpoints were
merged within a 75 m tolerance as a conservative geometry-repair step.
Substations located near the interior of a line-string component are incorporated by splitting the
line at the substation’s orthogonal projection point when the substation-to-line distance is within
10 m. These splits are subject to compatibility checks based on line ownership and voltage
family, and a short connector representing the actual substation-to-line projection line is added
when necessary. The processed geometries are then converted into an undirected weighted
graph �phys = (� phys, ℰphys) , by treating line-string vertices as graph nodes and consecutive
vertex pairs as length-weighted edges. For efficient distance calculations, each substation is
registered to the nearest node in �phys.

straight connections between each pair of directly connected substations. A pair is considered

any other substation. Undirected weighted edges are constructed with the weight being the
Dijkstra-computed along-grid shortest path length in �phys. This reduced graph � preserves the

2.5 Resource-Constrained Restoration Scheduling
2.5.1 Resource-Constrained Dispatch Model
Post-earthquake restoration is modeled as a resource-constrained multi-depot routing and
scheduling problem. The formulation enforces several operational constraints.
First, crew capacity ensures that the number of concurrent restorations cannot exceed the
number of crews. Each crew is anchored to a depot at initialization and executes a time-ordered
sequence of tasks. At any decision, each crew is characterized by its current location, and its
next available time. The system state is defined by the set of remaining damaged substations
and the crew states. After the repair is completed, the task is marked complete, the crew’s

2.5.2 Rule-based Restoration Sequencing
Rule-based sequencing is primarily based on predefined priority criteria derived from substation-
level network and service metrics. We evaluate seven strategies:
(1) Impact-first. Prioritizes structurally important substations to accelerate restoration of network
connectivity. Substations are ranked by impact centrality first, betweenness centrality second,
and node degree third.
(2) Betweenness-first. Prioritizes substations that serve as bridging nodes in the transmission
graph. Substations are ranked by betweenness centrality first and node degree second.
(3) Degree-first. Prioritizes substation connected to large number of other substations.
Substations are ranked by node degree first and betweenness centrality second.
(4) Closeness-first. Prioritizes substations with short paths of connections to the rest of the
network. Substations are ranked by closeness centrality first and node degree second.
(5) Impact-first (Population). Prioritizes substations expected to restore service to the largest
number of people. Substations are ranked by population impact, computed as a node-level
population-importance proxy from tract dependency weights and tract population.
(6) Hospital-first. Prioritizes substations serving tracts that contain any hospital. Substations are
ranked first by the number of mapped hospital-containing census tract links and second by total
mapped population.
(7) Random. Generates a fixed-seed random order of damaged substations and serves as a
reproducible baseline representing uncoordinated recovery.
Importantly, these policies differ only in task selection. All policies are evaluated under the same
operational constraints, allowing a clear comparison of decision logic.

3.1 Source-gated topology concentrates network vulnerability in
high-impact substations

32
Figure 2. Physical transmission network and reduced substation-level topology. (A) Processed
physical transmission-line network, showing CEC transmission-line geometries and substation
locations. (B) Reduced substation-level topology derived from the physical network. Each edge
represents direct along-network adjacency between two substations, defined by a physical-
network path containing no intermediate registered substation or substation projection anchor.
Edge weights retain the corresponding Dijkstra shortest-path lengths along the physical
transmission network; while displayed in straight lines, the links are schematic and do not
represent straight transmission corridors. (C) Percolation behavior of the reduced topology.
The network shown in Figure 2B is a reduced substation-level representation derived from the
processed physical transmission graph in Figure 2A. A reduced edge is retained only when two
registered substations are connected through the physical network and the intervening path
contains no other registered substation or substation projection anchor. Although the reduced
edges are displayed schematically as straight connections, each edge weight preserves the
corresponding along-network shortest-path distance in the physical graph. The resulting
connected network contains 92 nodes and 318 edges, with a mean degree of 6.91. Using along-
network distance as the edge weight, the mean shortest-path distance over all node pairs is
41.4 km. This reduction preserves the adjacency and distance relationships required for the
subsequent analyses of centrality, source connectivity, and restoration dynamics.
Substation importance depends on which centrality is considered. Degree centrality captures
local connectivity, but a high degree does not necessarily drive system-wide consequence.
Betweenness centrality highlights nodes that concentrate shortest-path routing and therefore
represent transmission bottlenecks. Impact (�2 -based) centrality captures the contribution of a
substation to global network fragmentation. Taken together, these centralities imply that
restoration priorities should not be guided solely by substations with large number of
transmission line connections.
Notably, when the power grid fragments into disconnected sub-networks, transmission lines
would no longer connect the available supply to demand across those sub-networks, so power
outage can persist even if some local assets remain functional. The percolation curves in Figure
2C track the network's LCC fraction as substations are removed. Under random removal,
connectivity decreases gradually, with only two more pronounced drops around the 33rd and 67th
node, respectively. In contrast, targeted removal takes out nodes ranked by the orders of
various centrality metrics calculated on the original graph, so each removal degrades the
network structure more than the random counterpart. Within the first 35 degree-targeted
removals, the LCC fraction drops to below 0.2, long before the random case reaches
comparable degradation. This indicates that the LCC decomposes much faster under targeted
removal, reflecting the concentrated impact on network connectivity from a small group of high-
importance substations.
This result indicates that the source-gated transmission topology is not uniformly vulnerable.
Network vulnerability is concentrated in a small group of substations whose disruption can
fragment the transmission network more rapidly than random outages. This topological
concentration provides the structural basis for later restoration-strategy comparisons, because

33
repairing highly connected or high-impact substations can influence not only local service
restoration but also the source connectivity of network components.

The strong performance of the hospital-first strategy is consistent with its prioritization of
substations linked to hospital-containing census tracts and its use of mapped population as a
secondary ranking criterion. These considerations place substations associated with
concentrated population and socially vulnerable populations earlier in the restoration sequence.
However, this result is scenario-specific and should not be interpreted as evidence that hospital
prioritization alone causes the improvement.
The key contrast is that different recovery strategies emphasize different service beneficiaries
and different portions of the recovery trajectory. Recovery performance depends on the
interaction among source-gated network service propagation, tract-substation dependency,
population exposure, and restoration logistics. The topology-oriented rules restore nodes that
are structurally important in the graph, but those nodes are not necessarily the substations with
the strongest tract-level service consequences. In the 2%-in-50-year scenario, the hospital-first

37
and impact-population-first rules reach �80 substantially earlier than the degree-, betweenness-,
closeness-, and impact-�2-first rules.
Across most strategies, population-and-SVI-weighted �80 is slightly earlier than or
approximately equal to population-weighted �80 , indicating that the restoration sequence
happens to recover many population-and-SVI-weighted service dependencies at least as
quickly as the population-weighted average. However, the magnitude of the population-SVI gap
varies by strategy. This difference is the key equity-relevant finding: restoration strategies do not
only differ in aggregate speed, but also in how their repair order aligns with the spatial
distributions of population exposure and social vulnerability.
Furthermore, strategy rankings depend on the recovery metric considered. The unconstrained
case provides the theoretical upper bound, with the earliest population- and population-and-SVI-
weighted �80 values of 41.85 and 41.80 h and the largest corresponding AUC values of 0.9291
and 0.9296. Among the logistics-aware strategies, hospital-first ranks first for both �80 and
AUC, reaching population- and population-and-SVI-weighted �80 values of 47.00 and 46.15 h
and AUC values of 0.9193 and 0.9204, respectively. The ordering of the next-best strategies

49.80 h, whereas impact-population-first ranks second for population-and-SVI-weighted �80 at

3.5 Sensitivity Analysis
The sensitivity analysis isolates the impact of key modeling assumptions on the baseline results.
The tested ranges are grouped into two categories, namely restoration-related assumptions and
topology-related assumptions. The restoration-related assumptions include crew availability and
restoration time scaling, which directly affect repair capacity and damage-conditioned
restoration duration. The topology-related assumptions include the IDW dependency threshold
and source-gate threshold, which affect tract-substation dependency mapping and source-gated
network accessibility.

4. Discussion
4.1 Contextual Comparsion
Because a probabilistic Los Angeles earthquake restoration scenario cannot be directly
validated against observations, the modeled Northridge scenario is compared with historical
Northridge restoration evidence as a contextual scale check. Çağnan et al. (2006), citing
LADWP’s post-Northridge restoration record, reported that approximately 50%, 75%, 90%, 95%,
and 100% of LADWP utility customers were restored within 7, 11, 19, 26, and 168 h,
respectively. The present modeled Northridge scenario gives a population-weighted �80 of
14.25 h for the unconstrained baseline and 14.55-15.25 h across logistics-aware restoration
strategies. Since the historical record does not directly report �80 , linear interpolation between
the reported 75% and 90% customer-restoration milestones gives an approximate historical
value of 13.7 h. The modeled values are therefore close to the historical partial-restoration scale.
The comparison also shows that the model should not be treated as a replay of the 1994 event.
The modeled Northridge �50 is shorter than the historical 50% customer-restoration milestone,
while the modeled �90 and �95 are longer. This mismatch is expected because the present
framework does not model distribution feeders, customer-level switching, or utility emergency
operating records directly. Instead, it evaluates a controlled source-gated transmission service
proxy. The main value of the comparison is therefore confirmation that the modeled partial-
restoration scale is not inconsistent with the historical Northridge restoration record.
The mechanisms underlying the modeled Northridge scenario are also consistent with prior Los
Angeles restoration modeling. Çağnan et al. (2006) found that Los Angeles residents may
experience earthquake-induced power outages lasting up to about 10 days, that rapidity risk
varies geographically, and that restoration can be constrained by repair materials and
restoration-process limitations. Cheng et al. (2024) further showed that substation damage is
the key driver of census-tract-level load-shed risk in Los Angeles, while Xu et al. (2007) treated
post-earthquake LADWP restoration as a scheduling problem intended to reduce average
customer outage time. The present study extends these prior findings by translating substation
damage into time-dependent tract-level service recovery and by evaluating how source-gated
topology, tract-substation dependency, utility yard travel, crew constraints, and restoration
prioritization rules reshape recovery outcomes. The tested prioritization rules show a trade-off
between optimizing overall network connectivity and minimizing the immediate impact of power
outages on the population. While the network centrality-based rules allow for prompt
reconstruction of the physical grid, the rules informed by tract characteristics perform better in
shortening the outage duration for highly populated and vulnerable tracts.
4.2 Future Work
The present framework is intended as a transparent, scenario-based decision-support
assessment for comparing how hazard, network dependency, repair logistics, and prioritization

44
assumptions shape tract-level recovery outcomes. Future work can extend the present
framework in several directions. First, the tract-level service representation can be refined by
incorporating distribution-network topology and utility customer-feeder connection data when
such data become available. This would allow transmission- and substation-level service
proxies to be linked more directly to feeder-level outage and restoration patterns. Second, the
tract-to-substation dependency model can be further improved by integrating utility service-
territory information, feeder maps, or empirical outage records, which would reduce reliance on
spatial proximity and topology-informed dependency assumptions.
The restoration component can also be expanded as more operational data become available.
Future studies could calibrate damage-conditioned restoration durations using utility repair
records, field inspection logs, or post-event restoration data. Road-network travel modeling
could also be enhanced by incorporating post-earthquake bridge damage, road closures,
congestion, emergency access restrictions, and time-varying travel conditions. In addition, the
restoration priority rules used here can be extended toward more realistic operational decision
models that account for utility-specific crew dispatch protocols, material availability, mutual-aid
coordination, and real-time damage information.
Further extensions can also strengthen the community-outcome interpretation. The recovery-
vulnerability typology developed in this study provides a descriptive classification of recurring
recovery profiles, and future work could examine the causal mechanisms linking infrastructure
dependency, social vulnerability, and delayed recovery. Hospital-service restoration can also be
refined by incorporating facility-level backup power, water supply, staffing, patient capacity, and
road accessibility, allowing future assessments to move from infrastructure-service access
toward a more comprehensive representation of hospital operational functionality.

45
5. Conclusion
This study presents an integrated tract-level assessment framework for post-earthquake
electric-power service recovery in the contiguous urban areas of Los Angeles County. By linking
seismic damage to substation assets, source-gated transmission network connectivity, tract-
substation service dependency, utility-yard and crew constraints, restoration-strategy
comparison, and recovery-vulnerability typologies, the framework connects physical
infrastructure disruption with community-level recovery outcomes. The analysis evaluates how
restoration decisions shape recovery trajectories and, under one representative strategy,
assesses how uneven recovery service availability and socio-economic characteristics interact
across census tracts, identifying areas where delayed restoration overlaps with higher social
vulnerability and disaster-risk exposure.
The results show that post-earthquake electric-power service recovery in the study area is
shaped by the interaction of network topology, tract-level dependency, repair logistics, and
social vulnerability. The source-gated topology concentrates network vulnerability in a limited
set of high-impact substations, while the unconstrained baseline shows that tract-level recovery
already varies spatially before crew-dispatch constraints are introduced. Under logistics-aware
restoration, utility yard locations, crew availability, travel time, and prioritization rules further
differentiate recovery outcomes.
The strategy comparison indicates that restoration priorities should be selected according to the
planning objective. Network centrality measures are useful for identifying substations that are
structurally important to transmission-network connectivity, but service-oriented strategies,
especially those based on population impact and hospital-related priority, minimize the durations
of service outages. GA-based strategies further show that milestone recovery, cumulative
recovery, and complete recovery can favor different restoration schedules and should therefore
serve as complementary performance metrics. Under the 2%-in-50-year scenario, the hospital-
first rule achieves the earliest population- and SVI-weighted �80 and the highest corresponding
AUC values among the logistics-aware strategies.
The recovery-vulnerability typology provides an additional community-level interpretation. The
clustering results show that delayed restoration and social vulnerability are not perfectly aligned.
Some socially vulnerable tracts recover relatively quickly in the modeled service network, while
some slower-recovery tracts are not among the most socially vulnerable. Therefore, the most
policy-relevant recovery-equity concern is concentrated in tracts where delayed restoration
overlaps with higher social vulnerability, older housing stock, and greater disaster-risk exposure.
The top recovery-vulnerability hotspots provide a more targeted screening output than either
recovery time or social vulnerability alone.
These findings address the study’s three core research questions. First, earthquake-induced
substation damage translates to tract-level disruption via the combined effects of spatially
varying ground motion, source-gated transmission network connectivity, and tract-substation
dependency, causing spatially uneven outages and differentiated layers of service importance

46
before repair logistics are considered. Second, utility-yard logistics, crew constraints, travel
times, and restoration priorities materially affect recovery. In the primary scenario, service-
oriented prioritization strategies, especially hospital-oriented choices, outperform network-
centrality rules in restoring power services to populations and critical hospital facilities. Finally,
clustering typologies and hotspots reveal that prolonged, vulnerability-amplified recovery occurs
in hotspot tracts around central Los Angeles County where delayed infrastructure restoration
overlaps directly with existing socioeconomic and disaster-risk burdens.
