records.text: Finally, recovery outcomes are interpreted using weighted recovery metrics, sensitivity analysis, and recovery-vulnerability typologies. Population- and vulnerability-weighted recovery trajectories are used to compare restoration strategies, while sensitivity analysis evaluates how major modeling assumptions affect recovery time and strategy-ranking stability. Simulated recovery indicators are then combined with social, demographic, built-environment, and hazard-related tract attributes. These features are standardized and fed into K-means clustering to identify census tracts where delayed recovery and vulnerability-related concerns coincide.

records.text: The pipeline integrates heterogeneous geospatial datasets. The physical power grid is represented using substation inventories and high-voltage transmission-line geometries from California Energy Commission (CEC) and Homeland Infrastructure Foundation-Level Data sources. Scenario-specific ground-motion fields are obtained from United States Geological Survey (USGS) ShakeMap products. Census tract boundaries are obtained from U.S. Census Bureau TIGER/Line data, with population and demographic attributes joined from the American Community Survey. Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) and National Risk Index (NRI) attributes are linked at the tract level, and hospital locations are obtained from California Health and Human Services open data.

records.section: 2.1.1 Topological Reconstruction of the Transmission Network
records.text: Transforming raw GIS geometries into a mathematically valid network graph is a critical prerequisite for subsequent analysis. Transmission line records containing multiple geometric components are first decomposed into individual line-string components, which consist of several vertex pairs, so that each component could be processed consistently. To reconcile spatial offsets between the line and substation layers, the true endpoints of each line-string component are snapped to nearby substations. Endpoints within 150 m are directly assigned to the nearest substation, whereas endpoints within 150 to 375 m are assigned only when the nearest substation is clearly preferred over the second-nearest one, based on both an absolute distance margin test and a nearest to second-nearest distance ratio test. To preserve existing line-line connectivity, when a junction vertex cluster satisfies the snapping criteria, all vertices in the cluster are moved together to the corresponding nearby substation. Substations located near the interior of a line-string component are incorporated by splitting the line at the substation’s orthogonal projection point when the distance is within the specified tolerance, which is 10 m at default. The processed geometries were then converted into an undirected weighted physical graph Gphys=(Vphys,ℰphys), by treating line-string vertices as graph nodes and consecutive vertex pairs as weighted edges. To facilitate distance calculations, substations are mapped onto the nodes inside Gphyswith coordinates.

records.text: Substation importance depends on which centrality is considered. Degree centrality captures local connectivity, but a high degree does not reliably translate into system-wide consequence. Betweenness centrality highlights nodes that concentrate shortest-path routing and therefore represent transmission bottlenecks. Impact (λ2-based) centrality captures the contribution of a substation to global network fragmentation. Taken together, these centralities imply that restoration priorities should not be guided solely by substations with large number of transmission line connections.

records.text: Notably, when the power grid fragments into disconnected sub-networks, transmission lines would no longer connect the available supply to demand across those sub-networks, so power outage can persist even if some local assets remain functional. The percolation curves in Fig. 2C track the network's largest connected component (LCC) fraction as substations are removed. Under random removal, connectivity decreases gradually, with only two more pronounced drops around the 33rd and 67th node, respectively.

records.text: In contrast, targeted removal takes out nodes ranked by the orders of various centrality metrics calculated on the original graph, so each removal is going to represent a greater impact on the network structure than the random counterpart. As a result, the LCC fraction falls much faster. For example, within the first 35 degree-targeted removals, the LCC fraction drops to below 0.2, long before the random case reaches comparable degradation. This indicates that the largest connected component decomposes much faster under targeted removal, reflecting the concentrated impact on network connectivity from a small group of high-importance substations.

records.text: This result indicates that the source-gated transmission topology is not uniformly vulnerable. Instead, network vulnerability is concentrated in a small group of substations whose disruption can fragment the transmission network more rapidly than random outages. This topological concentration provides the structural basis for later restoration-strategy comparisons, because repairing highly connected or high-impact substations can influence not only local service restoration but also the accessibility of source-connected network components.

records.section: 3.2 Unconstrained baseline recovery is spatially uneven across census tracts
records.text: The unconstrained baseline represents the recovery condition before explicit crew-routing and repair-dispatch constraints are imposed. As shown in Fig. 3A, tract-level T80 ranges from 35.8 to 45.8 h under the 2%-in-50-year scenario, with a large share of census tracts clustered near 43.25 h. The corresponding spatial distribution in Fig. 3B shows that the longest T80 values are concentrated in the northwestern portion of the study area. These results indicate that tract-level recovery is spatially uneven even before logistics-aware crew scheduling is introduced. The variation is generated by the combined effects of spatially heterogeneous substation damage, source-gated transmission connectivity, and tract-substation dependency structure. The unconstrained baseline therefore provides a reference condition for evaluating how utility yard travel, crew constraints, and restoration-prioritization strategies further reshape recovery outcomes in logistics-aware simulations.

records.section: 3.3 Logistics-aware restoration strategies produce different population- and vulnerability-weighted recovery outcomes
records.text: Fig. 5 and Table 4 compare recovery outcomes across the tested restoration strategies. Across most strategies, the SVI-weighted T80 is slightly earlier than or equal to its population-weighted counterpart, indicating that the weighted recovery metric for socially vulnerable tracts does not lag behind the general population metric under this scenario. Among the logistics-aware strategies, GA-Efficiency produces the fastest T80 among the tested cases, reaching 47.00 h for the population-weighted metric and 46.25 h for the SVI-weighted metric. This is approximately 4-5 h slower than the unconstrained baseline, indicating the additional delay introduced by crew, yard, and travel-time constraints. Among rule-based strategies, impact-first and hospital-first remain competitive. Impact-first reaches T80 at 49.35 h for the population-weighted metric and 47.70 h for the SVI-weighted metric, while hospital-first reaches T80 at 51.65 h and 49.90 h, respectively. In contrast, degree-first, closeness-first, betweenness-first, and random allocation produce longer recovery times, with population-weighted T80 values near 58-61 h. These results indicate that strategies based only on topological centrality do not necessarily maximize population- or vulnerability-weighted service recovery. Although such strategies may improve structural network robustness, they do not directly account for tract dependency, exposed population, vulnerable population, utility yard location, and travel-time constraints.

records.text: Table 4 also shows that strategy performance depends on the recovery metric being evaluated. As a reference, the unconstrained baseline reaches T80 at 41.90 h for the population-weighted metric and 41.85 h for the SVI-weighted metric. With the resource constraints considered, GA-Efficiency gives the fastest milestone recovery among the tested strategies, with T80 values of 46.45 h and 45.55 h for the population-weighted and SVI-weighted metrics, respectively. However, the highest cumulative recovery performance is achieved by GA-HospitalFirst, with AUC values of 0.9206 and 0.9214, indicating that the strategy that reaches the 80% recovery milestone fastest is not necessarily the same as the strategy with the strongest integrated recovery trajectory over the full evaluation horizon. Among rule-based strategies, Impact population first provides the strongest non-GA alternative, with T80 values of 49.35 h and 47.70 h and AUC values of 0.9197 and 0.9212 for the population-weighted and SVI-weighted metrics, respectively. It is also worth noticing that impact population first strategy achieves the shortest makespan, reflective of the nature of the strategy in restoring service to all popultion affected. In contrast, topology-oriented centrality rules and random allocation produce substantially slower T80 outcomes, generally near 58-61 h, showing that restoring structurally central substations alone does not necessarily maximize population- or vulnerability-weighted service recovery.

records.text: Overall, restoration strategy matters under logistics-aware scheduling. GA_Efficiency yields the fastest recovery among the tested strategies, while impact-first and hospital-first rule-based strategies provide competitive non-optimization alternatives. The comparison also shows that recovery performance cannot be inferred from network centrality alone, as population exposure, tract-substation dependency, and restoration logistics jointly shape service restoration.

records.section: 3.4 Recovery-vulnerability typologies identify where delayed restoration and social vulnerability coincide
records.text: Fig, 6 summarizes the recovery-vulnerability typologies identified for census tracts in the study area. K-means clustering identifies six tract groups, and Fig. 6 reports their profiles using selected recovery, built-environment, population, hazard-risk, asset-exposure, and social-vulnerability indicators, including recovery time (T80), pre-1970 housing ratio, population density, NRI risk score, NRI building value, and SVI composite score. These typologies are interpreted as recovery-disparity profiles.

records.section: 3.4 Recovery-vulnerability typologies identify where delayed restoration and social vulnerability coincide
records.text: Cluster 1 (n=34) represents tracts with the fastest modeled recovery, low hazard risk, relatively newer housing stock, and near-average social vulnerability. This profile suggests favorable modeled recovery conditions, likely associated with stronger source connectivity or more favorable tract-substation dependency. Cluster 2 (n=512) represents dense urban tracts with high social vulnerability, older housing stock, and lower building value, but with recovery times near the regional average. Cluster 3 (n=696) also represents socially vulnerable urban tracts and has the highest SVI composite score, yet its modeled recovery is slightly faster than average. Together, Clusters 2 and 3 show that high social vulnerability does not necessarily imply delayed modeled power-service restoration.

records.text: In contrast, Cluster 4 (n=377) forms the clearest delayed-recovery profile. These tracts have the longest recovery and high population density, but below-average SVI, pre-1970 housing ratio, and NRI risk score. This indicates that slower modeled recovery in Cluster 4 is more strongly associated with network-service dependency than with socioeconomic vulnerability. Cluster 5 (n=188) shows a more moderate profile, with slightly slower recovery, fairly old housing stock, near-average risk and building-value indicators, and below-average SVI. Cluster 6 (n=484) captures low-density tracts with high NRI risk, high building value, low SVI, and slightly slower-than-average recovery, indicating that recovery conditions are driven by hazard exposure  rather than social vulnerability.

records.section: 3.4 Recovery-vulnerability typologies identify where delayed restoration and social vulnerability coincide
records.text: The main interpretive result is that delayed recovery and social vulnerability are not perfectly aligned. Some socially vulnerable tracts recover relatively quickly, while some slower-recovery tracts are not among the most socially vulnerable. For this reason, a separate recovery-vulnerability hotspot analysis is used to identify tracts where multiple concern dimensions coincide. The hotspot score is constructed by converting four indicators—T80, pre-1970 housing ratio, NRI risk score, and SVI composite score—into percentile ranks and summing the ranks for each tract. The ten tracts with the highest composite scores are designated as recovery-vulnerability hotspots.

records.text: As shown in Fig. 6-D, the hotspot tracts identify locations where delayed modeled service restoration overlaps with higher social vulnerability, older housing stock, and greater natural-hazard risk. The hotspot analysis complements the cluster typology by isolating the locations where infrastructure recovery challenges and vulnerability-related concerns coincide most strongly. This provides a clearer basis for equity-informed, targeted restoration planning.

records.text: 3.5 Sensitivity Analysis
records.all_revision_text: 3.5 Sensitivity Analysis

records.text: This analysis is intended as a one-at-a-time sensitivity evaluation of major modeling assumptions. The tested ranges are grouped into two categories, namely restoration-related assumptions and topology-related assumptions. The restoration-related assumptions include crew availability and restoration time scaling, which directly affect repair capacity and damage-conditioned restoration duration. The topology-related assumptions include the IDW dependency threshold and source-gate threshold, which affect tract–substation dependency mapping and source-gated network accessibility. All sensitivity outcomes are evaluated relative to the baseline configuration.
records.all_revision_text: This analysis is intended as a one-at-a-time sensitivity evaluation of major modeling assumptions. The tested ranges are grouped into two categories, namely restoration-related assumptions and topology-related assumptions. The restoration-related assumptions include crew availability and restoration time scaling, which directly affect repair capacity and damage-conditioned restoration duration. The topology-related assumptions include the IDW dependency threshold and source-gate threshold, which affect tract–substation dependency mapping and source-gated network accessibility. All sensitivity outcomes are evaluated relative to the baseline configuration.

records.text: Fig. 7 and Table 5 summarize the sensitivity of population-weighted recovery time T80pop to restoration-related and topology-related assumptions under the 2%-in-50-year scenario. The results show that population-weighted recovery milestones are primarily controlled by the restoration-related assumptions. Crew availability produces the largest within-strategy change in T80pop, with a maximum shift of 49.70 h across the tested range. This reflects the direct effect of crew capacity on parallel repair execution and queuing delays. Restoration time scaling produces a comparable maximum shift of 45.10 h, because it directly stretches or compresses the duration of damage-conditioned restoration tasks across the system.

records.text: By contrast, topology-related parameters have smaller effects on aggregate T80pop. Varying the IDW dependency threshold changes how tract demand is distributed across substations, but its maximum effect on aggregate T80pop is only 1.10 h. This suggests that the population-weighted recovery milestone is relatively insensitive to moderate changes in weak tract–substation links after dependency weights are renormalized. The source-gate threshold has a larger but still moderate effect, with a maximum T80pop change of 5.70 h. This threshold affects which partially functional substations are allowed to participate in source-connected service propagation, but within the tested range it does not substantially alter the leading group of restoration strategies.

records.text: The sensitivity results also distinguish recovery-time uncertainty from strategy-ranking stability. Restoration time scaling, IDW threshold, and source-gate threshold preserve the baseline strategy ranking within the tested ranges. Crew availability is less rank-stable, with Spearman rank correlation ranging from 0.60 to 1.00. This indicates that crew scarcity can alter relative strategy performance by increasing the importance of repair sequencing, yard-to-task travel, and the spatial distribution of damaged substations. Overall, restoration-related assumptions primarily control the absolute duration of recovery, whereas topology-related assumptions mainly test the robustness of service-propagation and tract-mapping boundaries.

records.text: Contextural Comparsion
records.all_revision_text: Contextural Comparsion

records.text: Because a probabilistic Los Angeles earthquake restoration scenario cannot be directly validated against observations, the modeled Northridge scenario is compared with historical Northridge restoration evidence as a contextual scale check. Cagnan et al. (2006), citing LADWP’s post-Northridge restoration record, reported that approximately 50%, 75%, 90%, 95%, and 100% of LADWP customers were restored within 7, 11, 19, 26, and 168 h, respectively. The present modeled Northridge scenario gives a population-weighted T80 of 14.25 h for the unconstrained baseline and 14.55–15.25 h across logistics-aware restoration strategies. Since the historical record does not directly report T80, linear interpolation between the reported 75% and 90% customer-restoration milestones gives an approximate historical value of 13.7 h. The modeled values are therefore close to the historical partial-restoration scale.

records.text: The comparison also shows that the model should not be treated as a replay of the 1994 event. The modeled Northridge T50 is shorter than the historical 50% customer-restoration milestone, while the modeled T90 and T95 are longer. This mismatch is expected because the present framework does not model distribution feeders, customer-level switching, or utility emergency operating records directly. Instead, it evaluates a controlled source-gated transmission service proxy. The main value of the comparison is therefore confirmation that the modeled partial-restoration scale is not inconsistent with the historical Northridge restoration record.

records.text: The mechanisms underlying the modeled Northridge scenario are also consistent with prior Los Angeles restoration modeling. Cagnan et al. (2006) found that Los Angeles residents may experience earthquake-induced power outages lasting up to about 10 days, that rapidity risk varies geographically, and that restoration can be constrained by repair materials and restoration-process limitations. Cheng et al. (2024) further showed that substation damage is the key driver of census-tract-level load-shed risk in Los Angeles, while Xu et al. (2007) treated post-earthquake LADWP restoration as a scheduling problem intended to reduce average customer outage time. The present study extends these prior findings by translating substation damage into time-dependent tract-level service recovery and by evaluating how source-gated topology, tract–substation dependency, utility yard travel, crew constraints, and restoration prioritization rules reshape recovery trajectories.

records.text: Future Work
records.all_revision_text: Future Work

records.text: The present framework is intended as a transparent, scenario-based decision-support assessment for comparing how hazard, network dependency, repair logistics, and prioritization assumptions shape tract-level recovery outcomes. Future work can extend the present framework in several directions. First, the tract-level service representation can be refined by incorporating distribution-network topology and utility customer-feeder connection data when such data become available. This would allow transmission- and substation-level service proxies to be linked more directly to feeder-level outage and restoration patterns. Second, the tract-to-substation dependency model can be further improved by integrating utility service-territory information, feeder maps, or empirical outage records, which would reduce reliance on spatial proximity and topology-informed dependency assumptions.
records.all_revision_text: The present framework is intended as a transparent, scenario-based decision-support assessment for comparing how hazard, network dependency, repair logistics, and prioritization assumptions shape tract-level recovery outcomes. Future work can extend the present framework in several directions. First, the tract-level service representation can be refined by incorporating distribution-network topology and utility customer-feeder connection data when such data become available. This would allow transmission- and substation-level service proxies to be linked more directly to feeder-level outage and restoration patterns. Second, the tract-to-substation dependency model can be further improved by integrating utility service-territory information, feeder maps, or empirical outage records, which would reduce reliance on spatial proximity and topology-informed dependency assumptions.

records.text: The restoration component can also be expanded as more operational data become available. Future studies could calibrate damage-conditioned restoration durations using utility repair records, field inspection logs, or post-event restoration data. Road-network travel modeling could also be enhanced by incorporating post-earthquake bridge damage, road closures, congestion, emergency access restrictions, and time-varying travel conditions. In addition, the  restoration priority rules used here can be extended toward more realistic operational decision models that account for utility-specific crew dispatch protocols, material availability, mutual-aid coordination, and real-time damage information.

In addition, the  restoration priority rules used here can be extended toward more realistic operational decision models that account for utility-specific crew dispatch protocols, material availability, mutual-aid coordination, and real-time damage information.

records.text: Further extensions can also strengthen the community-outcome interpretation. The recovery-vulnerability typology developed in this study provides a descriptive classification of recurring recovery profiles, and future work could examine the causal mechanisms linking infrastructure dependency, social vulnerability, and delayed recovery. Hospital-service restoration can also be refined by incorporating facility-level backup power, water supply, staffing, patient capacity, and road accessibility, allowing future assessments to move from infrastructure-service access toward a more comprehensive representation of hospital operational functionality.

records.text: Conclusion
records.all_revision_text: Conclusion

records.text: This study presents an integrated tract-level assessment framework for post-earthquake electric-power service recovery in the Los Angeles region. By linking seismic damage to transmission/substation assets with source-gated network connectivity, tract–substation service dependency, utility-yard and crew constraints, restoration-strategy comparison, and recovery-vulnerability typologies, the framework connects physical infrastructure disruption with community-level recovery outcomes. The analysis therefore moves beyond aggregate grid functionality and evaluates how restoration decisions can produce uneven service recovery across census tracts, including areas where delayed modeled restoration overlaps with higher social vulnerability and disaster-risk exposure.
records.all_revision_text: This study presents an integrated tract-level assessment framework for post-earthquake electric-power service recovery in the Los Angeles region. By linking seismic damage to transmission/substation assets with source-gated network connectivity, tract–substation service dependency, utility-yard and crew constraints, restoration-strategy comparison, and recovery-vulnerability typologies, the framework connects physical infrastructure disruption with community-level recovery outcomes. The analysis therefore moves beyond aggregate grid functionality and evaluates how restoration decisions can produce uneven service recovery across census tracts, including areas where delayed modeled restoration overlaps with higher social vulnerability and disaster-risk exposure.

records.text: The results show that post-earthquake electric-power service recovery in the Los Angeles region is shaped by the interaction of network topology, tract-level dependency, repair logistics, and social vulnerability. The source-gated topology concentrates network vulnerability in a limited set of high-impact substations, while the unconstrained baseline shows that tract-level recovery already varies spatially before crew-dispatch constraints are introduced. Under logistics-aware restoration, utility yard locations, crew availability, travel time, and prioritization  further differentiate recovery outcomes across strategies.
records.all_revision_text: The results show that post-earthquake electric-power service recovery in the Los Angeles region is shaped by the interaction of network topology, tract-level dependency, repair logistics, and social vulnerability. The source-gated topology concentrates network vulnerability in a limited set of high-impact substations, while the unconstrained baseline shows that tract-level recovery already varies spatially before crew-dispatch constraints are introduced. Under logistics-aware restoration, utility yard locations, crew availability, travel time, and prioritization  further differentiate recovery outcomes across strategies.

records.text: The strategy comparison suggests that restoration priorities should be interpreted in relation to the planning objective. Network-oriented centrality measures are useful for diagnosing structurally important substations, but network-based priority rules do not necessarily produce the fastest population- or vulnerability-weighted service recovery. Service-oriented strategies, especially those based on population impact and hospital-related priority, provide stronger non-GA alternatives for restoring service to affected communities. GA-based strategies further show that milestone recovery and cumulative recovery can favor different schedules. The fastest T80 strategy is not necessarily the strategy with the highest AUC. This supports evaluating restoration performance using multiple metrics.

GA-based strategies further show that milestone recovery and cumulative recovery can favor different schedules. The fastest T80 strategy is not necessarily the strategy with the highest AUC. This supports evaluating restoration performance using multiple metrics.

records.text: The recovery-vulnerability typology provides a complementary community-level interpretation. The clustering results show that delayed restoration and social vulnerability are not perfectly aligned. Some socially vulnerable tracts recover relatively quickly in the modeled service network, while some slower-recovery tracts are not among the most socially vulnerable. Therefore, the most policy-relevant recovery-equity concern is concentrated in tracts where delayed modeled restoration overlaps with higher social vulnerability, older housing stock, and greater disaster-risk exposure. The top recovery-vulnerability hotspots provide a more targeted screening output than either recovery time or social vulnerability alone.

records.text: Future work can extend the framework by incorporating distribution-network topology, utility customer-feeder connection data, and observed outage or repair records when such data become available. The logistics component can also be refined by modeling post-earthquake road disruption, material availability, and mutual-aid coordination. A more targeted analysis could couple the tract-level service proxy with facility-level power-flow simulation to improve the representation of operational service restoration for hospitals and other critical facilities.

records.text: The 0.963 h term measures the direct removal of a station’s residual functionality under the production threshold. The connectivity indicator C also depends on that threshold: excluding an upstream station can create source-path loss elsewhere. Therefore, a small direct-threshold term does not prove that all network effects are independent of threshold assumptions. The formal .05/.50/.75 comparison is the relevant sensitivity evidence; no-threshold positive connectivity is exactly G0 under the current strictly positive residuals. State both facts. No new capacity model is required. [F, E]

records.text: In 2pc50/C57 the target Q4 group improves, yet Q1 and hospital-tract outcomes worsen versus hospital-first. State this as a targeted-priority tradeoff. records.section: 4.3  Relationship to prior work, historical context and applicability

records.text: The damage-propagation and logistics results together show how restoration sequencing changes both network-mediated losses and community service burden. records.text: The revised results are compared with prior Los Angeles seismic power-risk and restoration studies by electrical representation, decision problem, and spatial allocation. Candidate substations are restricted by utility context before distance weighting: SCE-compatible candidates for strict SCE tracts, LADWP-compatible candidates for strict LADWP tracts, and general eligibility for mixed or ambiguous tracts. Effective distance combines tract-to-access geographic distance with network distance through the retained station graph. Inverse-square weights are normalized, weights below 3% are removed, and the retained weights are renormalized.

records.text: Main content. Every station with DS > 0 becomes a repair task for that realization. Sampled repair duration remains attached to that task. records.text: 2.3 Source-connected modeled service
records.all_revision_text: 2.3 Source-connected modeled service

records.text: Main content. A station contributes modeled service when its damage-dependent functionality is above the functional threshold and it has a surviving path to at least one active Core source. Station service deficit is decomposed into local damage, threshold loss and source-path loss; tract service is the weighted sum across mapped stations and cumulative burden is integrated over the 480 h horizon.

records.text: Main content. Tracts are grouped into four equal-count social-vulnerability quartiles using the existing SOVI score, with Q4 denoting the highest-vulnerability quartile. records.section: 4.1 Restoration priorities, network propagation and community recovery
records.text: Content. The combined damage-propagation and logistics results connect station repair sequencing with both source-path loss and community service burden. Population, network and hospital-oriented priorities do not move all outcomes in the same direction, and the Degree-first contrast provides a clear example of improved source-path burden alongside higher total community burden. Crew scarcity and repair-duration uncertainty affect how much influence sequencing can exert.

records.section: 4.3 Relationship to prior Los Angeles studies, historical context and applicability
records.text: Content. Prior Los Angeles studies and the Northridge earthquake are used to compare modeling approaches and recovery timescales. The source-connectivity rule is a simplified service-availability check. The SCE capacity test shows that adding available planning limits changes the results only slightly for the substations with usable data, but it does not represent full power-flow or actual electricity delivery.

records.text: 4.4 Future extensions
records.all_revision_text: 4.4 Future extensions

records.text: Content. Feeder and outage records could strengthen local service attribution; source-specific available supply and station demand could support connected-island supply–demand analysis; a real bus/branch electrical case could support power-flow comparison; repair/access records could improve operational calibration. Explicit income data would be needed for low-income/very-low-income subgroup recovery analysis, and intervention-response or cost models would be needed before cluster typologies could support ranked financial, temporary-power, repair-resource or housing interventions.

records.all_revision_text: 9.1 Target and positioning for discussion

records.text: Recommended first target: International Journal of Disaster Risk Science (IJDRS). Its scope directly covers disaster risk, resilience, emergency response/recovery and the science–policy interface. The paper fits as a transferable disaster-recovery framework linking earthquake damage, infrastructure service disruption, resource-constrained restoration logistics and heterogeneous community outcomes. Los Angeles is the demonstration case; the source gate remains a topological service-availability proxy rather than an AC/DC power-delivery model. [J]

The framework remains the primary methodological contribution, with the Los Angeles results providing substantive findings rather than a workflow demonstration alone.

records.text: Current paper focus. The revision follows one physical-to-community chain: earthquake damage changes station functionality; surviving source paths determine modeled service availability; repair crews restore damaged stations under alternative priority rules; tract-level service and cumulative burden translate those system states into population, critical-service and vulnerability outcomes. The revised analysis emphasizes how restoration objectives redistribute recovery burden across communities. The network model represents service availability and does not constitute a full electrical power-flow model.

records.text: 2.1 Utility-compatible tract–substation mapping
records.all_revision_text: 2.1 Utility-compatible tract–substation mapping

records.text: Main content. Candidate substations are restricted by utility context before distance weighting: SCE-compatible candidates for strict SCE tracts, LADWP-compatible candidates for strict LADWP tracts, and general eligibility for mixed or ambiguous tracts. Effective distance combines tract-to-access geographic distance with network distance through the retained station graph. Inverse-square weights are normalized, weights below 3% are removed, and the retained weights are renormalized.
records.all_revision_text: Main content. Candidate substations are restricted by utility context before distance weighting: SCE-compatible candidates for strict SCE tracts, LADWP-compatible candidates for strict LADWP tracts, and general eligibility for mixed or ambiguous tracts. Effective distance combines tract-to-access geographic distance with network distance through the retained station graph. Inverse-square weights are normalized, weights below 3% are removed, and the retained weights are renormalized.

records.text: 2.2 Realization-specific repair execution
records.all_revision_text: 2.2 Realization-specific repair execution

records.text: Main content. Every station with DS > 0 becomes a repair task for that realization. Sampled repair duration remains attached to that task. Crew start time includes the crew’s next-available time and directed travel from its current location; completion returns raw station functionality to one and releases the crew at that station. The physical realization is common to every strategy.
records.all_revision_text: Main content. Every station with DS > 0 becomes a repair task for that realization. Sampled repair duration remains attached to that task. Crew start time includes the crew’s next-available time and directed travel from its current location; completion returns raw station functionality to one and releases the crew at that station. The physical realization is common to every strategy.

records.text: 2.3 Source-connected modeled service
records.all_revision_text: 2.3 Source-connected modeled service

records.text: Main content. A station contributes modeled service when its damage-dependent functionality is above the functional threshold and it has a surviving path to at least one active Core source. The 14 Core nodes are upstream boundary proxies; production analysis does not solve source dispatch, branch flow, voltage, reactive power or load shedding. Station deficit is decomposed into local damage, threshold loss and source-path loss; tract service is the weighted sum across mapped stations and cumulative burden is integrated over the 480 h horizon.

records.text: 2.5 Distributional measures
records.all_revision_text: 2.5 Distributional measures

records.text: Main content. Tracts are grouped into four equal-count social-vulnerability quartiles using the existing SOVI score, with Q4 denoting the highest-vulnerability quartile. The analysis reports population-weighted burden for each quartile, signed and absolute Q4–Q1 separation, population-weighted tract-burden Gini, and mean tract-level paired burden changes between policies. Negative paired burden change means lower burden under the candidate policy.

records.text: 2.7 SCE planning-capacity sensitivity
records.all_revision_text: 2.7 SCE planning-capacity sensitivity

records.text: Main content. The sensitivity uses documented SCE cumulative demand D and facility loading limit K where a retained station has an unambiguous one-to-one facility interpretation. Nineteen stations meet this criterion; nine multi-facility stations are not aggregated because no official aggregation rule was identified. The post-processing ceiling is applied to frozen trajectories and leaves unsupported stations at baseline. It is a static planning-peak stress test, not an electrical dispatch model.

records.section: 4.1 Restoration priorities, network propagation and community recovery
records.text: Content. The combined damage-propagation and logistics results connect station repair sequencing with both source-path loss and community service burden. Population, network and hospital-oriented priorities do not move all outcomes in the same direction, and the Degree-first contrast provides a clear example of improved source-path burden alongside higher total community burden. Crew scarcity and repair-duration uncertainty affect how much influence sequencing can exert.

Crew scarcity and repair-duration uncertainty affect how much influence sequencing can exert.

records.section: 4.3 Relationship to prior Los Angeles studies, historical context and applicability
records.text: Content. Prior Los Angeles seismic power-risk and restoration studies provide context by electrical representation, decision problem and spatial allocation. Northridge milestones provide recovery-timescale context. The source gate is interpreted as a necessary topological source-path condition, and the SCE planning-capacity sensitivity supplies a bounded external check for a supported subset without establishing full electrical adequacy for unsupported facilities, source supply, branch flow, voltage, dispatch or load shedding.

records.text: 4.4 Future extensions
records.all_revision_text: 4.4 Future extensions

records.text: Content. Feeder and outage records could strengthen local service attribution; source-specific available supply and station demand could support connected-island supply–demand analysis; a real bus/branch electrical case could support power-flow comparison; repair/access records could improve operational calibration. Explicit income data would be needed for low-income/very-low-income subgroup recovery analysis, and intervention-response or cost models would be needed before cluster typologies could support ranked financial, temporary-power, repair-resource or housing interventions.

records.section: 4.1 Restoration priorities, network propagation and community recovery
records.text: The damage-propagation and logistics results together show how restoration sequencing changes both network-mediated losses and community service burden. The Impact-first and Degree-first contrasts illustrate that source-path burden, population burden, hospital-tract burden and recovery milestones need not move in the same direction. records.section: 4.3 Relationship to prior Los Angeles studies, historical context and applicability
records.text: The revised results are compared with prior Los Angeles seismic power-risk and restoration studies by electrical representation, decision problem, and spatial allocation. Northridge milestones provide recovery-timescale context. The source gate is interpreted as a necessary topological availability condition, not sufficient electrical-delivery feasibility. Within the directly supported SCE subset, adding documented planning-capacity ceilings produces only small changes in the principal strategy comparisons; this does not establish adequacy for unsupported facilities, source supply, branch flow, voltage, dispatch or load shedding.

records.text: The damage-propagation and logistics results together show how restoration sequencing changes both network-mediated losses and community service burden. records.text: The typology results describe the community conditions that coexist with different recovery patterns, while the Vulnerability-first experiment quantifies redistribution under a targeted priority. Q4 improvement, impacts on Q1 and other groups, aggregate burden, hospital-tract burden, Q4–Q1 separation, and tract-burden Gini represent distinct outcomes. The C29/C57 comparison shows stronger redistribution when repair resources are more constrained. The typologies are not used to prescribe financial, temporary-power, repair-resource, or housing interventions, and SOVI quartiles are not interpreted as income groups.

records.section: 4.3 Relationship to prior Los Angeles studies, historical context and applicability
records.text: The revised results are compared with prior Los Angeles seismic power-risk and restoration studies by electrical representation, decision problem, and spatial allocation. Northridge milestones provide recovery-timescale context. The source gate is interpreted as a necessary topological availability condition, not sufficient electrical-delivery feasibility. Within the directly supported SCE subset, adding documented planning-capacity ceilings produces only small changes in the principal strategy comparisons; this does not establish adequacy for unsupported facilities, source supply, branch flow, voltage, dispatch or load shedding.

records.section: 4.3 Relationship to prior Los Angeles studies, historical context and applicability
records.text: Feeder and outage records would strengthen tract-level attribution. Source-specific available supply and station-level demand would support a connected-island supply–demand extension, while a real bus/branch electrical case would support full electrical-feasibility comparison. Repair, travel and access records would improve operational timing calibration. Explicit tract-level income data would be required for low-income and very-low-income recovery comparisons, and intervention-response/cost models would be required before cluster typologies could support ranked allocations of financial relief, temporary power, repair resources, or housing improvements.

records.section: 3.6 Sensitivity of mapping, source-gate and planning-capacity assumptions
records.text: Main content: Hospital-first M1 versus July mapping population-burden changes of +0.358, +0.231, +0.031 and −0.519 h across the four hazards; 246 tracts with mean paired 2pc50 shifts greater than 1 h in magnitude; cutoff and source-gate/source-threshold effects. The capacity test uses 19/92 one-to-one SCE stations, intersects 932/2315 tracts, and covers 0.2534 of population-weighted dependency mass. Only OLINDA 66/12 is capacity-binding. Across the nine 2pc50 cases, population-burden increments are 0.120–0.126 h; Impact–Hospital, Degree–Hospital and Vulnerability–Hospital contrasts change by −0.0004, +0.0037 and −0.0018 h, respectively, with no sign reversals.

records.section: 4.1 Restoration priorities, network propagation and community recovery
records.text: The damage-propagation and logistics results together show how restoration sequencing changes both network-mediated losses and community service burden. The Impact-first and Degree-first contrasts illustrate that source-path burden, population burden, hospital-tract burden and recovery milestones need not move in the same direction. Crew scarcity and repair-duration uncertainty control the amount of sequencing leverage.
records.all_revision_text: The damage-propagation and logistics results together show how restoration sequencing changes both network-mediated losses and community service burden. The Impact-first and Degree-first contrasts illustrate that source-path burden, population burden, hospital-tract burden and recovery milestones need not move in the same direction. Crew scarcity and repair-duration uncertainty control the amount of sequencing leverage.

records.text: 4.2 Vulnerability-targeted restoration and between-community outcomes
records.all_revision_text: 4.2 Vulnerability-targeted restoration and between-community outcomes

records.text: The typology results describe the community conditions that coexist with different recovery patterns, while the Vulnerability-first experiment quantifies redistribution under a targeted priority. Q4 improvement, impacts on Q1 and other groups, aggregate burden, hospital-tract burden, Q4–Q1 separation, and tract-burden Gini represent distinct outcomes. The C29/C57 comparison shows stronger redistribution when repair resources are more constrained. The typologies are not used to prescribe financial, temporary-power, repair-resource, or housing interventions, and SOVI quartiles are not interpreted as income groups.

records.section: 4.3 Relationship to prior Los Angeles studies, historical context and applicability
records.text: The revised results are compared with prior Los Angeles seismic power-risk and restoration studies by electrical representation, decision problem, and spatial allocation. Northridge milestones provide recovery-timescale context. The source gate is interpreted as a necessary topological availability condition, not sufficient electrical-delivery feasibility. Within the directly supported SCE subset, adding documented planning-capacity ceilings produces only small changes in the principal strategy comparisons; this does not establish adequacy for unsupported facilities, source supply, branch flow, voltage, dispatch or load shedding.

records.section: 4.3 Relationship to prior Los Angeles studies, historical context and applicability
records.text: Feeder and outage records would strengthen tract-level attribution. Source-specific available supply and station-level demand would support a connected-island supply–demand extension, while a real bus/branch electrical case would support full electrical-feasibility comparison. Repair, travel and access records would improve operational timing calibration. Explicit tract-level income data would be required for low-income and very-low-income recovery comparisons, and intervention-response/cost models would be required before cluster typologies could support ranked allocations of financial relief, temporary power, repair resources, or housing improvements.

records.text: Main content. Candidate substations are restricted by utility context before distance weighting: SCE-compatible candidates for strict SCE tracts, LADWP-compatible candidates for strict LADWP tracts, and general eligibility for mixed or ambiguous tracts. Effective distance combines tract-to-access geographic distance with network distance through the retained station graph. Inverse-square weights are normalized, weights below 3% are removed, and the retained weights are renormalized.

Inverse-square weights are normalized, weights below 3% are removed, and the retained weights are renormalized.

records.text: 2.5 Distributional measures
records.all_revision_text: 2.5 Distributional measures

records.text: Main content. Tracts are grouped into four equal-count social-vulnerability quartiles using the existing FEMA NRI v1.19 CDC-SVI-derived social-vulnerability score (historically stored as SOVI_SCORE), with Q4 denoting the highest-vulnerability quartile. The analysis reports population-weighted burden for each quartile, signed and absolute Q4–Q1 separation, population-weighted tract-burden Gini, and mean tract-level paired burden changes between policies. The hospital-linked outcome is the equal-weight mean modeled cumulative service loss across tracts containing retained hospital records; it is not hospital electricity delivery or clinical capacity. Negative paired burden change means lower burden under the candidate policy.

records.section: 4.1 Restoration priorities, network propagation and community recovery
records.text: Content. The combined damage-propagation and logistics results connect station repair sequencing with both source-path loss and community service burden. Population-, network- and hospital-oriented priorities do not move all outcomes in the same direction, and the Degree-first contrast provides a clear example of improved source-path burden alongside higher total community burden. Under the tested 2pc50 resource cases, policy contrasts are largest in the most crew-constrained condition and generally diminish as crew availability increases, while longer repair durations amplify Q4 and Q4–Q1 separation contrasts. The transferable mechanism is therefore greater sequencing leverage when restoration capacity is more constrained relative to workload; it is not claimed as a strictly monotonic or universal law.

records.section: 4.3 Relationship to prior Los Angeles studies, historical context and applicability
records.text: Content. Prior Los Angeles studies and the Northridge earthquake are used to compare modeling approaches and recovery timescales. The source-connectivity rule is a simplified service-availability check. The SCE capacity test shows that adding available planning limits changes the results only slightly for the substations with usable data, but it does not represent full power-flow or actual electricity delivery.

records.text: Content. Feeder and outage records could strengthen local service attribution; source-specific available supply and station demand could support connected-island supply–demand analysis; a real bus/branch electrical case could support power-flow comparison; repair/access records could improve operational calibration. Explicit income data would be needed for low-income/very-low-income subgroup recovery analysis, and intervention-response or cost models would be needed before cluster typologies could support ranked financial, temporary-power, repair-resource or housing interventions.

records.text: Abstract
records.all_revision_text: Abstract

records.text: Restoration sequences can redistribute community burdens even when their system completion times are similar. We compare four fixed sequences in a conditional Los Angeles study linking 302 repair-capable network assets, 57 pooled crews, and official Southern California Edison distribution-service candidates for 817 census tracts. Thirty-two paired damage and positive-duration realizations under a fixed 2%-in-50-year ground-motion field pass through event scheduling, completion-step asset restoration, source connectivity, and tract-level service-access intervals. Burden integrates the deficit of identifiable candidate availability; it does not measure observed customer outage hours. Relative to Hospital-first, two weighted-priority sequences reduce mean population-normalized burden by only 0.295 and 0.166 h, respectively. Their distributional effects differ: the hospital-dominant sequence reduces burden in the highest-vulnerability quartile by 0.413 h but increases it in the lowest by 0.117 h. An efficiency-oriented search comparator yields a lower burden Gini, 0.1765 versus 0.2187, while increasing mean burden in every quartile and population burden by 15.076 h. Doubling only severe-damage task durations raises this excess to 26.245 h. Varying the relative influence of two attachment classes preserves overall effect directions but alters some between-group relationships. The results distinguish reducing overall burden, benefiting higher-vulnerability communities, and equalizing burdens. They support conditional comparison of restoration decisions, rather than optimal equitable policies or predictions of delivered electricity.

An efficiency-oriented search comparator yields a lower burden Gini, 0.1765 versus 0.2187, while increasing mean burden in every quartile and population burden by 15.076 h. Varying the relative influence of two attachment classes preserves overall effect directions but alters some between-group relationships. The results distinguish reducing overall burden, benefiting higher-vulnerability communities, and equalizing burdens. They support conditional comparison of restoration decisions, rather than optimal equitable policies or predictions of delivered electricity.

records.text: 1 Introduction
records.all_revision_text: 1 Introduction

records.text: Restoration planning decides not only when a damaged infrastructure system finishes repair but also which communities wait during that process. A sequence that finishes slightly earlier need not reduce the accumulated burden experienced through the network. Nor does a more equal distribution of delay necessarily mean that any community is better off. These distinctions matter when limited crews must follow priorities set before the full consequences of uncertain damage and task durations are known.
records.all_revision_text: Restoration planning decides not only when a damaged infrastructure system finishes repair but also which communities wait during that process. A sequence that finishes slightly earlier need not reduce the accumulated burden experienced through the network. Nor does a more equal distribution of delay necessarily mean that any community is better off. These distinctions matter when limited crews must follow priorities set before the full consequences of uncertain damage and task durations are known.

records.text: Evaluating a restoration decision therefore requires several views of the same consequences: the accumulated population burden, the absolute burdens of different vulnerability groups, and the dispersion of those burdens. Comparing these views under shared damage and workload conditions separates differences due to the restoration sequence from differences due to the physical sample. It also makes a practical distinction visible: a decision can benefit a higher-vulnerability group without reducing the gap between groups, or reduce relative inequality while increasing everyone's group-average burden.

records.text: We examine these relationships in a Los Angeles case with a mixed-owner regional task network, a pooled crew scenario, and community outcomes in a conservatively defined Southern California Edison (SCE) candidate-service domain. Thirty-two physical realizations are shared across four fixed sequences. Two separate contrasts then change candidate influence and the relative duration of severe-damage tasks, allowing us to distinguish comparisons that persist under these conditions from group judgments that depend on them.

records.section: 1.1 Related research and the remaining question
records.text: Restoration research provides the logistics basis for this comparison. Çağnan et al. (2006) used discrete-event simulation to examine geographically varying restoration and resource bottlenecks in Los Angeles. Xu et al. (2007) optimized inspection, damage assessment, and repair schedules and evaluated them through restoration simulation. Cavdaroglu et al. (2013) connected infrastructure restoration and work-group scheduling rather than treating them as independent decisions. These studies show how sequencing, travel, resources, and uncertainty enter restoration decisions; they motivate retaining an explicit crew calendar when comparing community consequences.

It also calls for keeping absolute group burdens alongside relative gaps and inequality measures, since these quantities answer different questions about who benefits and who waits.

records.section: 1.1 Related research and the remaining question
records.text: Related physical and optimization studies address complementary parts of this problem. Cheng et al. (2024) coupled probabilistic earthquake damage with DC load-flow analysis and census-tract load shedding in Los Angeles. Toplu-Tutay et al. (2024) incorporated equity metrics into stochastic substation-hardening and power-flow decisions, and Jiang et al. (2025) addressed repair-duration uncertainty and equitable restoration decisions through a predict-then-optimize framework. Together, these studies establish approaches for quantifying physical consequences and embedding equity in decision objectives. The comparison pursued here focuses instead on how several evaluation criteria agree or conflict for the same fixed restoration decisions, and on which of those judgments depend on selected representation and workload assumptions.

records.text: 1.2 Research questions
records.all_revision_text: 1.2 Research questions

records.text: We ask three questions. First, how do Hospital-first, two weighted-priority sequences, and an efficiency-oriented search sequence differ in population burden and logistics under paired task uncertainty? Second, which vulnerability groups and tracts have lower or higher modeled burden, and do aggregate improvement, benefit to higher-vulnerability communities, and smaller group gaps coincide? Third, how do these contrasts change when proxy-attached service candidates receive less or more influence, or when severe-damage tasks take relatively longer?

Third, how do these contrasts change when proxy-attached service candidates receive less or more influence, or when severe-damage tasks take relatively longer?

records.text: The study contributes a paired set of comparison evidence linking these three questions. It quantifies whether small population-level differences conceal different group consequences, identifies who bears additional burden when relative inequality falls, and distinguishes overall comparisons that persist under the two targeted contrasts from group judgments that remain assumption-dependent. The resulting evidence supports conditional restoration decisions in a source-connected service-access model. Figure 1 summarizes the design, and Table 1 identifies the data and scenario assumptions under which the comparisons apply.

records.text: One damage vector and one duration vector were generated for each of 32 realization IDs and then stored. All four sequences use exactly the same physical vectors within each realization.

records.text: Only DS>0 assets become tasks. Undamaged assets do not enter the queue and have duration zero. At dispatch, duration is used to determine completion and the crew's next release, but it is never used to reorder pending tasks or choose a sequence.

records.section: 2.4 Event scheduling and effective network state
records.text: Each policy provides a complete 302-ID priority list. Removing DS0 assets yields the realization queue without reranking. The next task is assigned to the earliest available crew, with exact ties broken by ascending crew index. Travel is from that crew's origin for its first task and from its previous task thereafter. Arrival equals crew availability plus directed travel; completion equals arrival plus the stored realized duration. The crew is released at completion. Tasks are not preempted or shared between crews, and the queue does not adapt to future service outcomes.

records.text: Initial raw functionality is 1.00, 0.50, 0.09, 0.04, or 0.03 for DS0–DS4. A damaged asset retains its residual value until completion and becomes 1 at that event. There is no additional continuous repair CDF. Evaluation times are zero and the unique task-completion times, ending when all tasks finish. At each event, stations with raw functionality at least 0.5 define the functional subgraph. Components containing at least one active member of the fixed 21-node reference source set are retained. Effective state equals raw state inside those components and zero otherwise. Source membership is a reference availability scenario, not a verified list of operating Los Angeles generation sources. Source nodes can themselves be unavailable under the functionality threshold.

records.section: 2.5 Fixed sequences and the planning surrogate
records.text: Hospital-first orders the complete task domain by descending hospital-priority score, then population-priority score, then ascending station ID. Hospital priority uses a binary indicator for each of 47 tracts containing 53 retained hospital records; multiple records in one tract do not multiply its weight. This metric does not represent hospital operating capacity. Population and vulnerability priorities likewise originate from the 817-tract domain, propagate through candidate weights, and aggregate to A/B upstream assets. Vulnerability priority uses population multiplied by the retained Federal Emergency Management Agency National Risk Index (NRI) SOVI_SCORE, not the CDC Social Vulnerability Index. Components are independently min–max normalized over the 302 assets. Class C priority mass remains unassigned.

records.section: 2.5 Fixed sequences and the planning surrogate
records.text: For the other policies, service priority is a weighted average of population, hospital, and SOVI components. The Balanced weights are (1,3,1), the hospital-dominant HospFirst weights (1,20,1), and the Efficiency weights (1,1,1). Their makespan penalty coefficients are 0.5, 0.1, and 2.0. These are policy-design coefficients. In particular, 20 creates a strongly hospital-dominant archetype; it is not an empirical preference or an optimal societal weight. No network-importance term is included.

records.section: 2.5 Fixed sequences and the planning surrogate
records.text: The surrogate schedules all 302 assets using ex-ante expected workload: the probability-weighted positive duration over DS1–DS4. It uses the same crew origins and travel convention but never sees realized damage, realized duration, or community trajectories. For a sequence, completion benefit is the priority-weighted sum of max(504−completion,0), divided by 504 times total priority; fitness subtracts the makespan coefficient times makespan/504. This static additive objective does not directly optimize source-connected tract burden, T80, group gaps, or Gini. Scores are compared only under the same policy objective, not across differently weighted objectives.

records.section: 2.5 Fixed sequences and the planning surrogate
records.text: The retained genetic algorithm (GA) search used populations of 100, 100 generations, ordered crossover probability 0.8, inversion mutation probability 0.2, tournament size three, and ten seeds per policy. Examination of retained candidates identified deterministic priority-sorted initializers that attained the highest recorded Balanced and HospFirst fitness values. These two weighted-priority sequences are used here; they are not described as GA optima. Efficiency retains the highest-scoring saved finite-budget search sequence. Supplement S2 documents candidate retention, seed variation, deterministic incumbents, and the absence of any global-optimality guarantee.

Normalized burden N(r)=B(r)/R(r) is defined only for R(r)>0. Both B and N have time dimensions, but N is a normalized modeled availability deficit in hours, not observed resident outage time.

records.text: The first contrast changes only evaluation weights in tracts containing both A and B candidates. If A(r) and B(r) are their original weight totals, A weights are multiplied by R(r)/(A(r)+λB(r)) and B weights by λR(r)/(A(r)+λB(r)), with λ=0.5 or 2; λ=1 is the baseline. Class C mass, total resolved mass, official candidates, and attachments remain unchanged. Nonmixed tracts are unchanged. Sequences, priorities, physical vectors, sources, roads, and crews are fixed. This tests the evaluation of fixed decisions under two design stresses, not policy redesign under another mapping. The values are not an empirical range of true service shares.

records.text: The second contrast doubles only stored DS4 task durations, preserving DS0–DS3 values and every policy sequence. The event scheduler and subsequent state propagation are reexecuted because longer tasks alter crew release and later arrivals. No duration is redrawn and no policy is reoptimized for the new workload. This asks how the same decisions perform when severe-damage actions are relatively more time-consuming, not whether a different duration is empirically more accurate. It is not crossed with the A/B weighting contrast.

records.text: All strategy comparisons and changes in those comparisons are paired by realization ID. We report means, dispersion, median/IQR in the supplement, direction frequencies, and percentile 95% paired bootstrap intervals based on 10,000 resamples of the 32 realization units. The same resampling indices are used across policies and conditions. Tracts and policy runs are not treated as independent physical realizations. Intervals quantify variability in this sample under the stated model; they do not cover omitted physical processes, prove equivalence when crossing zero, or serve as simultaneous multiple-comparison guarantees. Effects are interpreted by magnitude and group consequences rather than a binary significance rule.

Ranking frequency, average effect, and effect uncertainty describe different aspects of performance; they do not identify one overall winner.

records.text: 4 Discussion
records.all_revision_text: 4 Discussion

records.text: 4.1 What the sequence comparisons establish
records.all_revision_text: 4.1 What the sequence comparisons establish

records.text: The principal result is a separation of decision criteria. Modest reductions in overall burden can have different group consequences; improvement for the highest-vulnerability quartile can increase the absolute gap when its baseline modeled burden is already lower; and lower Gini can coincide with higher burdens in every quartile. These observations are more informative than a single strategy ranking. They also show why T80, makespan, and a vulnerability-weighted aggregate should not be treated as interchangeable measures of community benefit.
records.all_revision_text: The principal result is a separation of decision criteria. Modest reductions in overall burden can have different group consequences; improvement for the highest-vulnerability quartile can increase the absolute gap when its baseline modeled burden is already lower; and lower Gini can coincide with higher burdens in every quartile. These observations are more informative than a single strategy ranking. They also show why T80, makespan, and a vulnerability-weighted aggregate should not be treated as interchangeable measures of community benefit.

records.text: Hospital-first and the two weighted-priority sequences are close in overall population burden. The small paired differences do not support claims of large policy superiority, nor do intervals spanning zero demonstrate equivalence. The HospFirst result is a specific distributional contrast, not an estimate of the causal effect of prioritizing hospitals. Its coefficients differ from the other policies in several respects, its ordering resembles Hospital-first, and hospital-tract burdens differ little. The study does not isolate a vulnerability-priority intervention or optimize fairness.

records.text: The interpretation of Efficiency is similarly bounded. A good score under its own static completion surrogate does not guarantee low source-connected community burden. Expected-workload decoding need not equal expected realized decoding: crew release, subsequent travel origins, and maximum completion are nonlinear in task durations. Moreover, an asset's completion may yield no immediate service benefit until another path or source becomes usable. The observed objective mismatch is therefore a comparison between distinct modeled quantities, not proof that optimization generally fails or that a particular social objective is undesirable.

records.text: 4.2 What the targeted comparisons add
records.all_revision_text: 4.2 What the targeted comparisons add

records.text: The A/B contrast addresses uncertainty in relative candidate influence while holding decisions fixed. Its stability in population-effect direction is useful, but limited: the group-level magnitudes and one signed gap depend on the weighting assumption. It does not validate named-system connectivity, true load shares, or omission of distribution-station damage. Recomputing priorities and searching anew under another mapping would answer a different question about policy design, which was not attempted.

Recomputing priorities and searching anew under another mapping would answer a different question about policy design, which was not attempted.

records.text: The DS4 contrast shows that a restoration assumption can alter relative community costs rather than merely stretching all recovery times. Stored task events for the two weighted-priority sequences show that doubling severe-damage durations changes crew assignments for roughly 220 tasks per realization, among an average of about 300 tasks, and increases mean arrival by approximately 32 h. This is evidence of changed event logistics, not a uniform rescaling of old trajectories. It does not establish that the doubled duration scenario is more realistic.

records.text: Saved interface integrals also permit accounting for modeled burden changes. For example, three upstream interfaces account for approximately 2.375, 2.363, and 2.027 h of Efficiency's baseline excess population burden; their contributions increase under longer DS4 tasks (Supplement S4). Such a decomposition identifies where a model's weighted deficit accumulates. It cannot, without adequate event evidence, establish that those stations' own repair order caused the differences, and it does not explain real neighborhood outcomes causally. We therefore avoid attributing results to unverified hospital geography, social mechanisms, or electrical bottlenecks.

records.text: 4.3 Scope and limitations
records.all_revision_text: 4.3 Scope and limitations

records.text: First, source-connected functionality is only a proxy for upstream availability. Connectivity may be informative when other electrical constraints are nonbinding, but their nonbinding status is not established here. Generation adequacy, capacity, protection, voltage, switching, and load shedding can change both levels and relative policy performance. Applying the same proxy to all policies does not eliminate that possibility. No comparison to historical restoration milestones is used as tract-level validation.

Generation adequacy, capacity, protection, voltage, switching, and load shedding can change both levels and relative policy performance. Applying the same proxy to all policies does not eliminate that possibility. No comparison to historical restoration milestones is used as tract-level validation.

records.text: Second, official candidate relationships improve the evidential basis over unrestricted distance allocation, yet equal weights and named-system attachments remain assumptions. Class A includes damage to its identified network asset; Class B omits separate downstream damage. The network and GIS sources span different epochs. Fifty-five tracts contain some unresolved candidate mass, and the twelve fully unresolved tracts are not a random sample that can safely be discarded in claims about the whole population. Population-weighted normalized burden describes the represented portion of partially identifiable tracts; it does not impute their unrepresented supply.

records.text: Third, the 302-asset task domain and the SCE outcome domain are not coextensive utility systems. Cross-owner crews are pooled, routes are static, and the 57-crew budget and on-site durations are uncalibrated scenarios. Roads remain usable; material shortages, mobilization, work shifts, task specialization, and distribution repairs are absent. This study compares sequences under one resource budget and cannot quantify the causal benefit of adding crews or recommend actual utility dispatch arrangements.

records.text: Fourth, the fixed hazard field, adopted fragility, independent conditional draws, and 32 existing realizations constrain inference. The two targeted contrasts do not constitute a full uncertainty analysis. Candidate correction was followed by reevaluation on the same sample, not a held-out test. Sequence selection remained ex ante with respect to the community objective, but the evidence should still be described as a limited paired comparison. No policy was further tuned to preserve a favorable ranking.

records.text: Finally, burden inequality is one distributional description, not a complete concept of equity. NRI-derived tract vulnerability does not identify individual need, and modeled time deficits do not measure hardship, health outcomes, access to backup power, or procedural justice. The four policy points do not trace a Pareto frontier. Stronger claims about equitable optimization or actual electricity recovery would require different objectives and additional physical and social evidence.

records.text: 5 Conclusion
records.all_revision_text: 5 Conclusion

records.text: Under the stated Los Angeles network and candidate-service conditions, fixed restoration sequences redistribute modeled community burden in ways not summarized by system completion or a single inequality statistic. Two weighted-priority sequences offer only small population-burden reductions relative to Hospital-first, while their group effects differ. The hospital-dominant sequence benefits Q4 while slightly increasing Q1 burden. An efficiency-oriented search sequence produces lower relative inequality but greater absolute burden in every quartile, without a clear mean makespan advantage.

Two weighted-priority sequences offer only small population-burden reductions relative to Hospital-first, while their group effects differ. The hospital-dominant sequence benefits Q4 while slightly increasing Q1 burden. An efficiency-oriented search sequence produces lower relative inequality but greater absolute burden in every quartile, without a clear mean makespan advantage.

records.text: The limited candidate-influence contrast preserves overall effect directions but changes some group relationships. Longer relative DS4 durations amplify Efficiency's additional community burden. These results support reporting absolute group levels, paired tract effects, and logistics costs together. They support a conditional study of how fixed recovery decisions allocate burden, not a claim to have found optimal equitable policies or predicted observed Los Angeles outages.
